title: ACT Prep
description: Free ACT Prep study guide: 8 units, 320 practice questions, 80 flashcards, quick reference, memory tricks, and a full practice exam. Completely free.

units.name: English Section Tactics

concepts.intro: Most ACT English comma questions test three patterns: unnecessary commas, missing commas around nonessential info, and comma splices.
b: Never place a single comma between a subject and its verb (e.g., 'The dog, ran' is wrong).
Nonessential clauses/appositives need commas on BOTH sides: 'My brother, a doctor, called.'
Essential (restrictive) clauses take NO commas: 'The book that I lent you is overdue.'
A comma splice (two independent clauses joined only by a comma) is always wrong — use a period, semicolon, or conjunction instead.
Never use a comma before a single coordinating conjunction joining two words or phrases (only before one joining two independent clauses).
Introductory phrases of 4+ words are usually followed by a comma.

concepts.intro: These three punctuation marks are ACT favorites because students often use them interchangeably when they shouldn't be.
b: A semicolon joins two independent clauses (each side must be a complete sentence).
A colon follows a complete independent clause and introduces a list, explanation, or quotation.
Never put a colon directly after a verb or preposition (e.g., NOT 'The ingredients are: eggs, milk.').
A pair of dashes can replace a pair of commas to set off nonessential information — but don't mix one dash and one comma.
Semicolons can also separate items in a complex list that already contains commas.
If you can't identify two independent clauses, a semicolon is wrong.

concepts.intro: When answer choices differ mainly in length, the ACT usually rewards the shortest option that preserves meaning and grammar.
b: Eliminate phrases that repeat an idea already stated, like 'combine together' or 'past history.'
Prefer active voice and direct phrasing over wordy constructions like 'due to the fact that' (use 'because').
Watch for answer choices that just add extra words without adding meaning — these are usually wrong.
'The reason why is because' is always redundant; choose 'because' alone.
Concise is not always correct — never cut information the passage needs for clarity.
Check whether a shorter option changes the meaning; if not, pick it.

concepts.intro: Agreement errors are hidden by long prepositional phrases or lists inserted between the subject and the verb.
b: Cross out prepositional phrases between subject and verb to find the true subject: 'The list of items (is/are) long' → 'list ... is'.
Collective nouns (team, group, family) usually take singular verbs on the ACT.
A pronoun must agree in number with its antecedent: 'Each student must bring their (wrong) → his or her/their own pencil' depends on style rules given.
Watch for vague pronouns with no clear antecedent — the ACT will flag ambiguous 'it' or 'they.'
Compound subjects joined by 'and' are plural; joined by 'or/nor' agree with the nearer subject.
Indefinite pronouns like 'each,' 'everyone,' and 'neither' are singular.

concepts.l: Rhetorical Skills: Transitions, Order, and Purpose
concepts.intro: About a quarter of English questions ask about the passage as a whole rather than grammar — these test logic and organization.
b: Transition words must match the logical relationship: contrast (however, although), addition (furthermore), cause/effect (therefore, as a result).
'ADD/DELETE' questions require you to check whether the sentence supports the paragraph's main point, not just whether it's interesting.
Sentence-order questions rely on pronoun references and time clues to find the correct sequence.
'Which choice best accomplishes the writer's goal' questions require rereading the stated goal, not just picking the best-sounding sentence.
Conclusion questions need a sentence that wraps up the paragraph's specific point, not a generic summary.
Always check one sentence before and after the underlined portion for context.

concepts.intro: The ACT frequently tests commonly confused words and possessive forms in the same passage.
b: 'Its' is possessive; 'it's' means 'it is' — never confuse them.
'Their' is possessive, 'there' is a location, 'they're' means 'they are.'
Plural possessive nouns ending in -s take only an apostrophe: 'the students' books.'
'Affect' is usually a verb (to influence); 'effect' is usually a noun (a result).
'Then' refers to time/sequence; 'than' is used for comparisons.
Singular possessive nouns take apostrophe + s, even if the noun ends in s: 'James's car.'

keyFacts: The English test has 75 questions in 45 minutes across 5 passages — about 9 minutes per passage.
Roughly 40% of questions test grammar/usage (punctuation, agreement) and 60% test rhetorical skills (style, organization, strategy).
When choices vary only in punctuation, identify whether the surrounding clauses are independent or dependent first.
'NO CHANGE' is correct about 25% of the time — don't avoid it just because it feels too easy.
traps: Choosing the most 'formal-sounding' answer, not the grammatically correct or most concise one.
Adding a comma wherever you would naturally pause when reading aloud, rather than following a comma rule.
Answering rhetorical 'writer's goal' questions based on general quality of writing, not the stated goal.
Fixing only the underlined error and ignoring how the sentence fits the surrounding paragraph.

units.name: Math Section Tactics

concepts.intro: When a question asks for a specific numeric value and gives answer choices, working backward from the choices is often faster than solving algebraically.
b: Start with choice (C) or (B) — the middle value — since answers are usually ordered numerically, so you can adjust up or down.
Plug the choice back into the original word problem, not into a derived equation.
Backsolving is fastest for problems involving one variable and multiple steps of arithmetic.
Avoid backsolving on problems asking for an expression or a variable in terms of another variable.
Combine backsolving with estimation to eliminate 2-3 choices immediately.
For 'least/greatest possible value' questions, test the extreme answer choices first.

concepts.intro: For problems with variables in both the question and the answer choices, substituting simple numbers avoids abstract algebra errors.
b: Choose easy, non-trivial numbers like 2 or 3 — avoid 0 and 1, which can make multiple answers look correct.
Compute the target value using your chosen number(s) before checking answer choices.
Plug the same number(s) into every answer choice and eliminate any that don't match your target.
If two answers match, pick a different set of numbers to break the tie.
This method works especially well on percent, ratio, and 'in terms of' problems.
For geometry, picking numbers for side lengths can simplify area/perimeter comparisons.

concepts.intro: The ACT math section leans heavily on a small set of geometry formulas that appear across many question types.
b: Area of a triangle: (1/2) × base × height; area of a circle: πr²; circumference: 2πr.
Pythagorean theorem: a² + b² = c², used constantly in right-triangle and distance problems.
Special right triangles: 45-45-90 (sides x, x, x√2) and 30-60-90 (sides x, x√3, 2x) save time versus the Pythagorean theorem.
Sum of interior angles of a polygon: (n − 2) × 180°.
Slope formula: (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁); slope-intercept form: y = mx + b.
Distance formula: √[(x₂−x₁)² + (y₂−y₁)²], derived directly from the Pythagorean theorem.

concepts.intro: Function notation and systems of equations questions reward recognizing structure quickly rather than brute-force solving.
b: f(x) notation just means 'plug x into the function' — evaluate step by step, innermost operation first.
For systems of equations, use substitution when one variable is already isolated; use elimination when coefficients line up.
A quadratic in the form ax² + bx + c = 0 can often be solved faster by factoring than by the quadratic formula.
When a graph question gives f(x) and asks about f(x) + k or f(x − h), remember: +k shifts up, −h shifts right.
Inequalities flip direction only when multiplying or dividing both sides by a negative number.
For 'solve for x in terms of y' questions, isolate x using standard algebra, then match the answer format given.

concepts.intro: A calculator can speed up arithmetic but can also cost time if used on problems better solved with reasoning.
b: Not every problem requires a calculator — number-sense and logic problems are often faster by hand.
Use the calculator to check answers after solving algebraically, not as your primary problem-solving tool.
Store useful values (like π or a computed ratio) in calculator memory for multi-step problems.
For probability and combinatorics, know factorial and combination functions if your calculator supports them.
On graphing questions, you can graph both sides of an equation and find intersection points to solve.
Convert fractions to decimals only when needed for comparison — exact fractions avoid rounding errors.

concepts.intro: The ACT tests basic statistics and probability concepts, often embedded in tables, graphs, or word problems.
b: Mean = sum of values ÷ number of values; median is the middle value when data is ordered.
Probability = (favorable outcomes) ÷ (total possible outcomes), always between 0 and 1.
For independent events, multiply individual probabilities: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B).
Range = maximum − minimum; a single outlier affects the mean far more than the median.
When reading tables/graphs, check the axis labels and units before selecting a value.
Weighted averages require multiplying each value by its weight (frequency) and dividing by the total weight.

keyFacts: The Math test has 60 questions in 60 minutes — pace roughly one question per minute, but the first 20 are usually easier and faster.
Calculators are allowed for the entire math section (per current ACT policy), but strategic use matters more than calculator speed.
Roughly 60% of questions cover algebra and functions, and roughly 40% cover geometry, statistics, and probability combined.
Skipping a hard question and returning later beats spending 5 minutes stuck on one problem.
traps: Solving with full algebra when plugging in numbers or backsolving would be faster and less error-prone.
Choosing 0 or 1 when plugging in numbers, which can make several answer choices appear correct.
Forgetting to flip an inequality sign when multiplying or dividing by a negative number.
Misreading a graph's scale or units, leading to an answer that's off by a factor of 10 or more.

units.name: Reading Speed Strategies

concepts.l: Passage Mapping Instead of Full Reading
concepts.intro: With only about 8-9 minutes per passage including questions, skimming for structure beats reading every word closely.
b: Read the first and last sentence of each paragraph carefully; skim the middle for supporting detail.
Jot a 3-5 word margin note capturing each paragraph's main idea as you go.
Note where the author's opinion or a turning point ('however,' 'but,' 'in contrast') appears — these are common question targets.
Underline or mentally flag proper nouns, dates, and numbers since detail questions often ask about them.
Don't try to memorize the passage — build a mental map you can return to using line references.
Spend no more than 3-4 minutes reading before moving to the questions.

concepts.l: Order of Passages and Question Triage
concepts.intro: You control the order you tackle the four passages, and picking wisely protects your overall score.
b: Passage order rotates (Literary Narrative, Social Science, Humanities, Natural Science) but difficulty varies by test-taker strength, not fixed difficulty.
Do your strongest passage type first to bank points and build confidence/time cushion.
Within a passage, answer line-reference and detail questions before big-picture/inference questions, since they're faster to locate.
If a question stumps you after ~20 seconds of rereading, mark it and move on — return only if time remains.
Never leave a question blank on the ACT — there's no penalty for guessing, so always fill in an answer.
Save the hardest passage type for last so a time crunch affects it, not your strongest section.

concepts.intro: Most reading questions point you to a specific location — using that window efficiently is the core reading skill tested.
b: Always reread a few lines before AND after the cited line reference — the answer is rarely only in the exact line quoted.
For vocabulary-in-context questions, plug your own word into the sentence before looking at answer choices.
Watch for words that have a common meaning and a less common, more precise meaning — the ACT usually tests the less common one.
'According to the passage' questions require textual proof, not outside knowledge or assumptions.
'It can be reasonably inferred' questions still require direct textual support — inference is a small logical step, not a guess.
When two answers seem right, choose the one most directly supported by the text, not the one that sounds smartest.

concepts.intro: Many big-picture questions ask why the author included something or how they feel about the topic.
b: Identify whether the overall tone is objective/informative, critical, or admiring within the first two paragraphs.
'Why did the author include paragraph X' questions test function, not content — ask what job the paragraph does.
Watch for shifts in tone signaled by contrast words; the tone before and after a shift may differ.
Rhetorical questions and figurative language in Literary Narrative passages often reveal the narrator's attitude.
In paired-passage sets, compare each author's stance on the same issue — questions often ask how they'd respond to each other.
Avoid choices that describe an extreme tone (e.g., 'furious,' 'ecstatic') unless the text clearly supports that intensity.

concepts.intro: ACT Reading wrong answers follow predictable patterns that can be spotted and eliminated quickly.
b: Eliminate answers that are true statements but don't answer the specific question asked (out of scope).
Eliminate extreme language ('always,' 'never,' 'completely') unless the passage explicitly supports it.
Eliminate answers that reverse a relationship stated in the passage (e.g., swapping cause and effect).
Eliminate 'half-right' answers that start correctly but include one incorrect detail.
Eliminate answers that bring in outside knowledge not stated in the passage, even if factually true.
The correct answer is usually a restatement of the text in different words, not new information.

keyFacts: The Reading test has 40 questions across 4 passages in 35 minutes — about 8-9 minutes per passage including questions.
There is no penalty for wrong answers, so every question should be answered, even if guessed.
Paired passages (two shorter related passages) appear in one of the four slots and include comparison questions.
Correct answers are almost always directly supported by the text, not by outside knowledge or opinion.
traps: Rereading the entire passage from scratch to answer each question instead of using line references.
Picking an answer because it sounds sophisticated rather than because the text supports it.
Confusing a detail question (needs proof from the text) with an inference question (needs a small logical step).
Getting stuck on a hard vocabulary-in-context question instead of substituting your own word first.

units.name: Science Reasoning

concepts.intro: ACT Science has three recurring passage formats, and knowing which one you're facing tells you how to attack it.
b: Data Representation passages present graphs/tables and ask you to read and interpret trends directly.
Research Summaries describe one or more experiments and ask about design, variables, and results.
Conflicting Viewpoints presents 2-3 scientists' differing hypotheses about the same phenomenon and asks you to compare them.
Data Representation and Research Summaries questions rarely require outside science knowledge — the answer is in the figures.
Conflicting Viewpoints requires careful reading since there's more text and less data to scan.
Identify the passage type in the first few seconds by scanning for graphs/tables versus paragraphs of viewpoints.

concepts.intro: Most Science questions can be answered without reading the passage text at all — just the figures.
b: Identify the independent variable (x-axis) and dependent variable (y-axis) before reading any question.
Check units and scale on every axis — a jump from 10-20-40 is not evenly spaced.
For multi-line graphs, note which line represents which condition using the legend before comparing them.
Interpolation (estimating a value between two plotted points) is common; extrapolation (beyond the data) is riskier and less often correct.
When a question references 'Table 1' or 'Figure 2,' go straight to that figure — don't reread the whole passage.
Trends (increasing, decreasing, constant, or no clear pattern) are the most frequently tested relationship type.

concepts.intro: Research Summaries test understanding of how experiments are structured, not memorized science facts.
b: The independent variable is what the experimenter changes; the dependent variable is what is measured.
A control group/trial is used as a baseline for comparison and typically has no treatment applied.
Variables held constant across trials are 'controlled variables,' meant to isolate the effect of the one variable being tested.
Comparing two experiments usually means identifying exactly what changed between them and what stayed the same.
'Why did the researchers include a control?' answers should reference isolating the effect of the independent variable.
Repeating trials increases reliability of results, not necessarily accuracy of a single measurement.

concepts.intro: This passage type tests reading comprehension applied to scientific arguments rather than data analysis.
b: Make a quick note of each scientist's core claim and the evidence/mechanism they cite for it.
Identify what all viewpoints agree on versus where they diverge — agreement points are common question targets.
'Which scientist would most likely agree with the following statement' questions require matching the statement's logic to one viewpoint's reasoning.
New data presented in a question can support one viewpoint and contradict another — check both.
Avoid using outside scientific knowledge to judge which viewpoint is 'more correct' — the ACT only tests reading comprehension here.
Track terminology differences between viewpoints, since one scientist's specific term may not apply to another's model.

concepts.intro: A small amount of outside science knowledge — mostly about method and measurement — does appear on the ACT.
b: A hypothesis is a testable, falsifiable prediction, not simply a guess.
Correlation between two variables does not by itself establish causation.
Common metric units (grams, liters, meters, °C) may appear; know basic prefixes like kilo- (1000x) and milli- (1/1000).
A directly proportional relationship means both variables increase together; inversely proportional means one increases as the other decreases.
Significant figures/precision in a table can hint at measurement reliability but rarely require calculation.
The scientific method process: observation, hypothesis, experiment, analysis, conclusion.

keyFacts: The Science test has 40 questions across 6-7 passages in 35 minutes — roughly 5 minutes per passage.
About 90% of questions can be answered directly from the given data without outside science knowledge.
Data Representation and Research Summaries passages together make up most of the section; Conflicting Viewpoints is usually just 1 passage.
Answering figure-based questions before reading passage text often saves significant time.
traps: Trying to apply memorized science class facts instead of reading the given data or viewpoint carefully.
Confusing which axis is the independent variable versus the dependent variable on a graph.
Assuming a trend continues beyond the plotted data range (extrapolating) when the question only supports interpolation.
Mixing up two scientists' viewpoints in Conflicting Viewpoints passages because their terminology overlaps.

units.name: Writing (Optional) Overview

concepts.intro: The ACT Writing prompt always presents an issue and three different perspectives on it, asking you to develop your own position.
b: You get 40 minutes to read the prompt, plan, write, and proofread a single essay.
The three given perspectives typically represent different value trade-offs — read all three before choosing your position.
You may agree fully with one perspective, partially agree, or synthesize elements of two — full agreement isn't required for a high score.
Your essay must explicitly discuss the relationship between your own perspective and at least one of the given perspectives.
Prompts are usually about broad social or ethical issues (technology, education, community) accessible without specialized knowledge.
Spend the first 5 minutes planning before writing — a clear plan matters more than a fast start.

concepts.intro: ACT Writing is scored by two graders on four domains, each on a 1-6 scale, then combined into a final 2-12 score.
b: Ideas and Analysis: the depth and clarity of your argument and your engagement with multiple perspectives.
Development and Support: how well you use specific reasoning, examples, and evidence to back up claims.
Organization: a clear structure with logical progression, effective transitions, and a strong intro/conclusion.
Language Use: sentence variety, word choice, and control of grammar/mechanics appropriate for a timed essay.
All four domains are weighted equally, so a paper with a brilliant idea but poor organization won't earn a top score.
The essay score does not count toward your Composite score — it is reported separately.

concepts.l: Building a Strong Thesis and Structure
concepts.intro: A clear five-paragraph structure with an explicit thesis gives graders an easy way to award points.
b: State your own perspective clearly in the introduction, including how it relates to the given perspectives.
Use one body paragraph per major point of support, each starting with a clear topic sentence.
Dedicate at least one paragraph to directly analyzing a perspective you disagree with or complicate.
Use concrete examples (historical, personal, or hypothetical) rather than vague generalizations.
End with a conclusion that reinforces your thesis and briefly acknowledges the broader significance of the issue.
Avoid restating the prompt word-for-word in your introduction; paraphrase it briefly instead.

concepts.intro: The highest-scoring essays don't just state an opinion — they actively compare and evaluate the given perspectives.
b: Summarize each of the three perspectives accurately before critiquing or building on any of them.
Explain the underlying value or assumption behind each perspective (e.g., prioritizing efficiency vs. fairness).
Show how your own view addresses a limitation or blind spot in at least one given perspective.
Avoid a simple 'perspective one is right, the others are wrong' approach — nuanced engagement scores higher.
Use transition phrases like 'while this view assumes X, it overlooks Y' to signal analytical depth.
Address counterarguments to your own position, then explain why your reasoning still holds.

concepts.intro: With only 40 minutes total, allocating time deliberately across planning, writing, and revising prevents an unfinished essay.
b: Spend about 5 minutes reading the prompt and the three perspectives carefully.
Spend about 5 minutes outlining your thesis and body paragraph structure.
Spend about 25 minutes writing the full essay, aiming for roughly 4-5 paragraphs.
Reserve the last 5 minutes for proofreading grammar, spelling, and clarity — not for major rewrites.
Write legibly; graders can only score what they can read within their limited grading time.
If running short on time, prioritize finishing your conclusion over adding another body paragraph.

keyFacts: The Writing test is optional and not included in your Composite score, but many colleges request it.
The essay is scored on a 2-12 scale, averaging four domain scores from two graders each scored 1-6.
You must engage with at least one of the three given perspectives, not just state your own opinion in isolation.
Length alone doesn't earn points — a well-organized, well-supported shorter essay beats a rambling long one.
traps: Simply restating all three perspectives without ever developing your own distinct argument.
Ignoring the given perspectives entirely and writing a generic essay on the topic.
Ending abruptly without a conclusion because too much time was spent on body paragraphs.
Using only vague, general claims with no specific examples or reasoning to back them up.

units.name: Timing Frameworks

concepts.intro: Each ACT section has a fixed time limit and question count, so knowing your per-question budget prevents running out of time.
b: English: 75 questions / 45 minutes ≈ 36 seconds per question.
Math: 60 questions / 60 minutes = 1 minute per question, front-loaded easier at the start.
Reading: 40 questions / 35 minutes ≈ 8-9 minutes per passage (including reading time).
Science: 40 questions / 35 minutes ≈ 5 minutes per passage.
Writing (optional): 1 essay / 40 minutes, split roughly 5/5/25/5 across reading, planning, writing, and proofreading.
Build in a 2-3 minute buffer per section for review of flagged/skipped questions.

concepts.intro: Using checkpoints during a section prevents discovering you're behind schedule only when time is called.
b: Check the clock at the midpoint of each section — you should be roughly at the halfway question count.
In Math, expect to be through question 30 by the 30-minute mark; adjust pace if significantly behind.
In Reading/Science, use the passage transition as a natural checkpoint rather than checking the clock mid-passage.
If behind pace, switch to answering only questions you can solve in under 30 seconds, and guess/flag the rest.
If ahead of pace, use the extra time to double check flagged questions rather than slowing down overall.
Practice with a visible timer during prep so checkpoint pacing becomes automatic on test day.

concepts.intro: Answering every 'easy for you' question first, then returning for harder ones, maximizes points per minute.
b: On your first pass through a section, answer every question you can solve quickly and skip (but mark) the rest.
Never leave a bubble blank on your first pass — fill in a guess, then revisit if time allows.
On the second pass, spend remaining time only on marked/flagged questions, starting with ones that seem most solvable.
This strategy protects against running out of time before reaching easier questions later in a section.
Two-pass works especially well on Math, where difficulty roughly increases with question number.
For Reading/Science, apply two-pass within each passage rather than across the whole section.

concepts.l: Guessing Strategy and No Penalty for Wrong Answers
concepts.intro: The ACT's scoring rewards guessing over leaving blanks, which should shape late-section decisions.
b: There is no penalty for incorrect answers, so every question should have a bubble filled in before time is called.
If you must guess blindly, pick one 'letter of the day' (e.g., always C) and use it consistently for speed.
Eliminating even one implausible choice before guessing meaningfully raises your odds versus a blind guess.
Reserve the last minute of any section to bubble in guesses for all remaining unanswered questions.
Never spend more than 60-90 seconds total deciding whether to guess on a single stuck question.
Guessing strategically (eliminating options) beats guessing randomly, but both beat leaving a blank.

concepts.intro: The whole ACT (excluding Writing) runs about 2 hours and 55 minutes, and stamina management matters as much as per-section pacing.
b: Standard test order is English, Math, (short break), Reading, Science, (Writing if taken).
A 10-15 minute break typically occurs after Math — use it to hydrate, stretch, and mentally reset, not to review answers.
Fatigue tends to hit hardest in Science (the last multiple-choice section), so practice full-length tests to build stamina.
Avoid perfectionism on any single section; a poor Math section shouldn't be allowed to bleed into your Reading mindset.
Simulate full-length, timed practice tests at least 2-3 times before test day to calibrate real pacing.
Track your actual per-section timing in practice to identify which section needs the most pacing work.

keyFacts: Total ACT time (without Writing) is about 2 hours 55 minutes across English, Math, Reading, and Science.
Math is the only section giving a full 1 minute per question on average; others require faster pacing.
There is no penalty for wrong answers on the ACT, so guessing is always better than leaving a blank.
A short break follows Math, before Reading and Science — plan hydration and a stretch around it.
traps: Spending 3+ minutes on a single hard question instead of marking it and moving on.
Leaving questions blank because you didn't reach them, instead of guessing before time is called.
Ignoring pacing checkpoints and only realizing you're behind schedule near the end of a section.
Using break time to obsess over a previous section instead of resting for the next one.

units.name: Question Type Patterns

concepts.l: English: Grammar vs. Rhetorical Skills Questions
concepts.intro: English questions fall into two broad families that require different approaches: fixing errors versus improving effectiveness.
b: Grammar/usage questions (punctuation, agreement, verb tense) have one objectively correct answer based on rules.
Rhetorical skills questions (organization, style, strategy) ask which choice best fits the writer's purpose or the paragraph's logic.
Underlined-portion questions test grammar most often; 'whole passage' questions (often at the end) test rhetorical skills.
Tense consistency questions require checking the tense used elsewhere in the same paragraph, not just the sentence.
Questions asking to 'add a sentence that provides...' require matching content to a specific stated purpose.
'Which choice is NOT acceptable' questions flip the usual approach — find the option that breaks a rule.

concepts.intro: ACT Math questions repeat a handful of formats; recognizing the format quickly speeds up solving.
b: 'Solve for x' questions want a numeric or algebraic answer — check whether the choices are numbers or expressions.
'Which of the following must be true' questions require checking ALL cases, not just one example that seems to work.
'Which of the following could be true' questions only need ONE valid example to justify an answer.
Word problems often bury a trap by asking for a value related to, but not identical to, what you first solve for (e.g., solving for x when the question asks for x+3).
Diagram-based geometry problems may not be drawn to scale — never estimate an answer purely from the picture.
'Approximately' in a question signals it's fine (and often faster) to estimate rather than calculate exactly.

concepts.l: Reading: Detail, Inference, and Big-Picture Questions
concepts.intro: Reading questions split into three main categories, each requiring a different search strategy in the text.
b: Detail questions ask 'what does the passage state' — the answer is a near-paraphrase of an explicit sentence.
Inference questions ask 'what can reasonably be concluded' — the answer requires one small logical step beyond the text.
Big-picture questions ask about the main idea, purpose, or tone of an entire passage or paragraph.
Vocabulary-in-context questions test the meaning of a word AS USED in that specific sentence, not its most common definition.
Comparison questions in paired passages ask how the two authors' views relate — look for explicit points of agreement/disagreement.
Function questions ask why the author included a specific detail, example, or paragraph.

concepts.l: Science: Trend, Comparison, and Prediction Questions
concepts.intro: Science questions almost always ask you to read a trend, compare data points, or predict an unlisted value.
b: Trend questions ask how one variable changes as another changes — read the direction directly off the graph/table.
Comparison questions ask you to evaluate two or more trials, figures, or scientists' claims against each other.
Prediction questions ask for a value not directly shown — check whether it falls within the data range (interpolation, safer) or beyond it (extrapolation, riskier).
'Which figure supports the statement' questions require matching a claim to specific numbers, not general impressions.
Questions with 'if only Table 1 were used' logic test whether you understand what each specific data set does and doesn't show.
Questions about experimental flaws or improvements test understanding of controls and variables, not outside science facts.

concepts.intro: Learning to recognize a question type from its first few words saves seconds you can reinvest across the section.
b: 'According to the passage/table' signals a direct-lookup question with no inference required.
'It can be inferred/reasonably assumed' signals you need a small logical extension of stated facts.
'The author's primary purpose' or 'the main idea' signals a big-picture question — don't over-focus on one detail.
'Which choice best maintains the sentence pattern' or 'is most consistent with the writer's tone' signals a style-matching question.
'If the experiment were repeated with...' signals a hypothetical scenario question requiring you to apply, not just read, the data.
Questions naming a specific paragraph, line, figure, or table number should send you straight there, not to the whole passage.

keyFacts: Each of the four multiple-choice sections has 4 answer choices (A-D or F-J), unlike the SAT's 4-option format for all questions too.
Recognizing whether a question is asking for an explicit detail versus an inference changes how much text-searching you need to do.
'Must be true' requires checking every case; 'could be true' requires only a single valid example.
Odd-numbered English answer choices are labeled A-D and even-numbered ones F-J to make bubble sheets easier to read.
traps: Treating an inference question like a detail question and demanding the exact wording appear in the text.
Assuming a 'must be true' answer is correct after checking only one example instead of all possible cases.
Extrapolating far beyond a graph's data range and treating the result as equally reliable as interpolation.
Ignoring the specific figure/table/line reference in a question and rereading the entire passage instead.

units.name: Full Practice Workflow

concepts.intro: A structured multi-week plan targeting weak areas outperforms unfocused, last-minute review.
b: Take one full-length diagnostic test first to identify your baseline score and weakest section.
Allocate more weekly study time to your lowest-scoring section, but don't neglect strong sections entirely.
Plan for at least one full-length, timed practice test every 1-2 weeks to track progress under real conditions.
Leave the final 2-3 days before the test for light review only — avoid new content or heavy cramming.
Space practice sessions across multiple days rather than cramming, since spaced repetition improves retention.
Track score trends across practice tests, not just the raw score of the most recent one.

concepts.intro: How you review practice questions matters more for improvement than how many you complete.
b: For every missed question, identify WHY you missed it: content gap, careless error, timing pressure, or misread question.
Keep an error log categorizing mistakes by type (e.g., comma rules, inference questions) to spot patterns.
Redo missed math and science questions without looking at the solution first, to test if it was a fluke or a true gap.
For English/Reading, go back to the passage and locate the exact textual evidence for the correct answer.
Review correct-but-slow answers too — a right answer that took 3 minutes reveals a pacing weakness.
Revisit your error log weekly to confirm previously weak categories are improving.

concepts.intro: Practicing under conditions that mirror test day reduces surprises and anxiety on the actual exam.
b: Take full-length practice tests in one sitting with only the official short break, not spread across days.
Use an actual answer sheet and bubble in answers (or a timed digital interface) rather than circling in the book.
Practice with the same calculator you'll bring on test day so you're fluent with its functions.
Sit in a quiet space free of phone notifications to build focus stamina for the full ~3 hours.
Time each section strictly with a stopwatch or timer, stopping exactly when time is called, even mid-question.
Simulate the optional Writing test too if you plan to take it, since it adds 40 minutes of additional stamina demand.

concepts.intro: Understanding how ACT scores are calculated helps set realistic, motivating goals.
b: Each of the four main sections is scored 1-36; the Composite score is the rounded average of all four.
A raw score (number correct) converts to a scaled score via a table that varies slightly by test form.
Colleges often superscore, averaging your best section scores across multiple test dates — check each target school's policy.
Set a target Composite score based on the middle 50% range of admitted students at your target colleges.
Focus on your single lowest-scoring section for the biggest potential Composite score gain.
A 1-2 point Composite gain often requires answering just a few more questions correctly across sections.

concepts.intro: Physical preparation and a calm mindset are as much a part of an ACT strategy as content mastery.
b: Confirm your test center, start time, and required ID the night before, and lay out materials in advance.
Bring an approved calculator, several No. 2 pencils, a photo ID, and your admission ticket.
Eat a balanced meal beforehand and bring an approved snack for the break to maintain energy.
Arrive early to reduce pre-test stress; rushing in late increases anxiety and error rates.
Use brief breathing resets between sections rather than dwelling on a section you felt went poorly.
Remember one weak section doesn't determine your Composite — stay focused on the section in front of you.

keyFacts: Consistent, spaced full-length practice tests are the single best predictor of ACT score improvement.
An error log that categorizes WHY you missed each question turns practice into targeted improvement.
The Composite score is the rounded average of the four 1-36 section scores (English, Math, Reading, Science).
Many colleges superscore the ACT, so strategic retesting focused on your weakest section can raise your Composite.
traps: Taking many practice tests without ever reviewing why questions were missed.
Cramming new content in the final 1-2 days instead of resting and doing light review.
Ignoring pacing during practice tests by pausing the clock, which hides real timing weaknesses.
Focusing study time evenly across all sections instead of prioritizing the lowest-scoring one for the biggest gain.

Guess immediately without reading it

o: Yes, a quarter point per wrong answer

Yes, but only on Math

quiz.q: Why should you check the clock at set checkpoints during a section?
o: To decide in advance which questions you will leave blank
To measure how many answers you have already gotten correct
To reset your timer so each question gets equal minutes
To confirm you're on pace to finish before time runs out

quiz.q: Why reserve the last 1-2 minutes of a section?
o: To reread the hardest passage one more time
To rework your earliest answers from scratch again
To begin previewing the next section's questions
To transfer and verify bubble-sheet answers

o: No, passages must be completed in the printed order
Yes, so start with the easiest passage to bank points
Only on Science, since Reading passages are locked in order
Only after you have answered every question on the first passage

quiz.q: A student spends 5 minutes on one hard English question out of 45 minutes total. What's the main risk?
o: Running out of time for the remaining questions
No risk, since English has no time limit
It guarantees a lower Reading score
It only affects the essay score

quiz.q: What is the recommended approach to pacing on ACT Math, where difficulty tends to increase?
o: Spend extra time on early questions so that no easy points are lost
Move quickly through easier early questions to save time for harder later ones
Divide the time equally so every question gets exactly the same minutes
Start with the hardest final questions while your mind is freshest

quiz.q: If a student consistently runs out of time on Science, what's a good fix?

Practice timed passages to build faster data-reading speed
Read every passage's full text twice before looking at questions
Take untimed practice only until the content feels comfortable

o: Recheck flagged or uncertain answers
Start the next section's questions
Close your eyes and wait
Erase all your answers and redo them

quiz.q: Why is a consistent timing plan important across all four ACT sections?
o: Only Math and Science have limits while others are untimed
Each section is scored separately with its own strict clock
Unused time from one section is added to the next one
One total time limit covers the whole test as a single block

quiz.q: A student wants to practice pacing for Reading. What's an effective drill?

Read passages with no time limit at all
Only read the last paragraph of each passage
Skip practicing pacing since scores don't depend on it

quiz.q: What happens to unanswered ACT questions?
o: They cost a quarter point each, so blanks are safer than guesses
They count as no worse than a wrong answer since there's no guessing penalty
They are scored as partially correct if the section is mostly finished
They are dropped from the section's total so scaled scores rise
quiz.e: Since there's no penalty for wrong answers, leaving a question blank has no advantage over guessing.

quiz.q: Which timing habit helps avoid a rushed final few minutes?
o: Checking progress at the midpoint of the section
Waiting until 2 minutes remain to check the time for the first time
Ignoring the clock completely
Only checking time on the last question
quiz.e: A midpoint check lets you adjust pace with plenty of section time still remaining.

quiz.q: On the Math section, when should a student consider skipping a question temporarily?
o: When it's taking noticeably longer than the average ~1 minute pace
When it includes a graph or figure, since those take the most time
When it appears in the first third, since early items count less
When you do not recognize the topic from your school coursework
quiz.e: If a question is eating far more than the average time-per-question, moving on and returning later protects overall pacing.

quiz.q: What is a realistic per-passage time budget for Science given 35 minutes and 6-7 passages?
o: About 5 minutes per passage
About 15 minutes per passage
About 1 minute per passage
About 20 minutes per passage

quiz.q: Why might a student choose to answer the shortest Reading passage first?
o: To save the hardest passage for last since it is worth more points
To follow the required rule that the shortest passage is done first
To secure quick points and build momentum before longer passages
To reduce the number of questions that must be answered overall
quiz.e: Passage order is flexible, so starting with a shorter passage can bank points efficiently.

quiz.q: What's the danger of spending too much time perfecting the wording of an ACT essay's introduction?
o: It lowers the Ideas score because introductions are weighed heavily
It forces the scorer to read the essay twice as carefully
It can use up the 60-minute limit needed for revising the body
It can eat into the 40-minute limit needed for full development

quiz.q: A student has finished all 75 English questions with 5 minutes left. What should they do?
o: Review flagged or uncertain answers
Immediately begin the Math section
Stop working entirely
Erase and rewrite every answer

quiz.q: What is one benefit of timing yourself on individual passages during practice?
o: It reveals which passage types are slowing you down most
It shows which answer letter appears most often as correct
It predicts the exact scaled score you will earn on test day
It proves which passages will appear on your real exam

quiz.q: Why does the ACT test date-day schedule typically start with English rather than Math?

The proctor rotates the starting section at each test center each date
The order is Math, English, Science, Reading, then optional Writing
The ACT's fixed order is English, Math, Reading, Science, then optional Writing

quiz.q: What should a student do if they realize halfway through Math that they're behind pace?
o: Slow down on the rest to guarantee accuracy even if some go blank
Speed up on remaining easier questions and flag hard ones for later
Go back to question one and recheck every earlier answer first
Skip the easy items and tackle only the hardest remaining questions

quiz.q: On test day, why is it useful to know your section timings before you sit down?
o: So you can set internal pacing goals and reduce surprises under time pressure
Because timing isn't announced during the real test
So you can request extra time automatically
It isn't useful; timing is the same for every test taker regardless of practice

quiz.q: Which is the best description of 'banking time' as a pacing strategy?
o: Saving all difficult questions for the final minutes of the section
Spending extra minutes on easy questions to make sure none are missed
Borrowing unused minutes from a different section to use when needed
Finishing easy questions quickly to build a time cushion for harder ones later
quiz.e: Banking time means moving efficiently through easy questions to create a buffer for tougher ones.

quiz.q: A student always runs out of time on the same section across multiple practice tests. What should their timing plan target?
o: Extra timed drills specific to that section's pacing
Ignoring that section since it's clearly a lost cause
Spending more time on sections where they already finish early
Taking the section untimed on the real test

quiz.q: What is a reasonable order to attempt Science passages if two or three feel unusually dense?
o: Work through them in printed order since reordering is not allowed
Save the densest passages for last after completing more approachable ones
Answer the densest ones first because they are worth more points
Spend equal time reading all passages before answering any questions

quiz.q: Why is consistent full-length timed practice important for building ACT pacing skills?
o: It lets you memorize the questions that tend to repeat on actual exams
It replaces content review because every skill is practiced automatically
It trains stamina and pacing under conditions matching the real test's strict clocks
It shows your scaled score will rise by a set amount for each test taken
quiz.e: Realistic timed practice conditions your internal clock to match the real section limits.

quiz.q: If a student has extra time left in Reading after finishing all questions, what's the least useful choice?
o: Rechecking the answers they had flagged as uncertain during the section
Reviewing the line references on the trickiest questions to confirm choices
Double-checking that each bubble matches the intended answer on the sheet
Rereading answered easy questions they were already fully confident about
quiz.e: Time is better spent on uncertain items than re-verifying answers you were already fully confident about.

quiz.q: What is the relationship between total section time and number of questions used to estimate pace?
o: Multiplying minutes by questions gives the number of seconds allowed for the passage
Dividing total minutes by total questions gives an average time-per-question benchmark
Subtracting questions from minutes shows how many items can be skipped safely
Dividing the composite score by minutes gives the pace needed on each item
quiz.e: Average time-per-question (minutes divided by questions) is the standard pacing benchmark.

quiz.q: Which best summarizes the core idea behind ACT timing frameworks?
o: Sections share a flexible total time budget, so students can shift minutes freely between sections to maximize how many questions they answer correctly
Each section has a fixed time and question count, so a deliberate pacing plan per section maximizes attempted, accurate answers
Question counts vary by test date while time limits stay fixed, so a single universal pacing rule works best for maximizing accurate answers
Each section has a fixed question count but no time limit, so a careful reading plan per section maximizes the number of accurate answers
quiz.e: Because each section has strict, separate time limits, a per-section pacing plan is the foundation of ACT time management.

quiz.q: Why is it useful to know the exact number of questions in a section before test day?
o: It tells you how many questions can be left blank without lowering your score
It lets you predict which answer letter is most likely to appear most often
It shows how many questions each topic will contribute to your final composite
It lets you set mental pacing markers (e.g., 'by question 20 I should be X minutes in')
quiz.e: Knowing both time and question count lets you set concrete pacing checkpoints throughout a section.

quiz.q: A student answers all 40 Science questions with 10 minutes still remaining. What likely happened?

The section was administered incorrectly

quiz.q: On ACT English, about how often is 'NO CHANGE' the correct answer?

Roughly a quarter of the time

More than half the time

quiz.q: When English answer choices differ mainly by length, what's usually true?
o: The option with the most commas is usually the best choice
The shortest grammatically correct option is usually best
The option that adds the most descriptive detail is usually best
The option that matches the surrounding sentence length is usually best

quiz.q: What does an 'EXCEPT' or 'LEAST' question require you to find?
o: The single answer choice that best matches every stated criterion
The answer choice that is most strongly supported by the passage
The one answer choice that does NOT fit the stated criteria
The answer choice that appears most often among the other options
quiz.e: In EXCEPT/LEAST questions, every wrong choice actually satisfies the criteria; only the correct answer fails to.

quiz.q: How should you determine the meaning of a word in a vocabulary-in-context question?
o: Plug each choice into the sentence and judge by the passage's specific context
Choose the meaning that matches the word's most familiar dictionary definition
Pick the most advanced synonym, since the author uses elevated language
Select the choice that sounds closest to the word itself in spelling or sound
quiz.e: Context, not the word's most familiar dictionary sense, determines the correct choice.

quiz.q: What can most ACT Science 'Data Representation' questions be answered from?
o: Outside science coursework knowledge only
Directly reading the given graph or table
Guessing based on answer choice length
Memorized formulas
quiz.e: Data Representation questions are typically answerable straight from the provided figures, no outside knowledge required.

quiz.q: On ACT Math, when should you pick 'cannot be determined'?
o: Only when the given information is truly insufficient to solve the problem
Whenever the problem looks complicated enough that solving may take too long
Whenever a variable remains in the problem after you simplify the expression
Whenever two of the answer choices produce the same value when tested
quiz.e: 'Cannot be determined' is often a trap for solvable problems — only choose it when the math genuinely lacks enough information.

quiz.q: What must be true for an answer to satisfy a Reading 'must be true' question?
o: It matches a common idea about the topic from general reading
It repeats key phrases that appear in the passage's first paragraph
It is consistent with at least one scenario the passage allows
It holds under every scenario the passage supports
quiz.e: A 'must be true' claim is eliminated by any single scenario in the passage where it fails to hold.

quiz.q: What do paired-passage comparison questions typically ask you to do?
o: Decide which of the two authors writes with better evidence
Summarize the main events described in only the first passage
Identify where the two authors' viewpoints agree or disagree
Determine which passage was written first, based on its style
quiz.e: Comparison questions test how well you can locate each author's stance and compare them directly.

quiz.q: How should a 'writer's goal' question be answered?
o: Based on whether the choice is the smoothest and most vivid sentence overall
Based on whether the choice is the most concise of the options presented
Based on whether the choice repeats information already in the paragraph
Based on whether the choice specifically accomplishes the stated goal in the question
quiz.e: These questions are graded strictly against the stated purpose, not general writing quality.

quiz.q: When two Reading answer choices differ by one qualifying word like 'always' vs. 'often', what's the safer approach?
o: Check the passage carefully — extreme qualifiers are frequently wrong unless directly supported
Pick the option with the stronger qualifier, since it sounds more confident and complete
Treat the two as equivalent and decide using the order of the answer choices
Skip both options and select whichever remaining choice avoids any qualifier
quiz.e: Extreme language needs explicit textual support; softer qualifiers are usually the safer default.

quiz.q: What is a reliable sign that a chosen ACT Reading answer is correct?
o: It agrees with what most people already believe about the topic overall
It sounds like something the author would say based on the title alone
It can be traced directly back to specific wording or ideas in the passage
It covers more ground than the other choices and sums up all the topics
quiz.e: Correct Reading answers are always traceable to specific textual evidence, not just impressions.

quiz.q: On ACT Science, what is a common trap involving two similar-looking answer choices?
o: They usually differ by a small but meaningful detail that changes correctness
They are usually paraphrases of one another so either choice earns credit
They typically differ by units that the test does not count when scoring
They are almost always taken from different passages in the same set
quiz.e: Similar-looking choices often hinge on one precise detail from the data — read carefully before choosing.

quiz.q: What pattern do redundancy questions on ACT English test?
o: Recognizing and keeping repeated words for added emphasis in a sentence
Choosing the longest option that restates the idea with precise wording
Spotting transitions that connect two ideas in different paragraphs
Recognizing and eliminating unnecessary repeated words or phrases
quiz.e: Redundancy questions reward trimming repeated ideas — e.g., 'returned back' should become 'returned.'

quiz.q: What is the recommended approach to a Science question asking about a trend beyond the plotted data range?
o: Recognize it as interpolation and read the value directly from the graph
Recognize it as extrapolation and reason cautiously from the visible trend
Assume the trend levels off at the last plotted point and stays constant
Treat it as unanswerable and select the choice that mentions no change
quiz.e: Predicting beyond given data is extrapolation — use the established trend's direction to reason toward the best-supported choice.

quiz.q: What does 'interpolation' mean in an ACT Science context?
o: Estimating a value between two known data points
Estimating a value beyond the plotted data range
Ignoring the data table entirely
Combining two unrelated experiments
quiz.e: Interpolation is estimating within the range of already-known data points, as opposed to extrapolating beyond it.

quiz.q: In a Conflicting Viewpoints Science passage, what should you check before answering a scientist-specific question?
o: Which scientist's viewpoint appears to be best supported by the table
Which scientist presents the longest explanation in the passage text
Which scientist's viewpoint the question is actually asking about
Which of the two explanations seems more likely to be true in reality
quiz.e: Conflicting Viewpoints questions require attributing the correct reasoning to the specific scientist named.

quiz.q: What is a strong strategy for a Math question that says 'for all values of x'?
o: Test the answer choices with simple numbers like 0, 1, or -1
Solve for x by isolating it on one side of the equation first
Substitute a single value such as 2 and trust that choice completely
Look for the answer choice that contains the same variable terms
quiz.e: Plugging in simple test values is often the fastest way to check which choice holds for all x.

quiz.q: What does a 'function' question about a sentence or paragraph typically ask?
o: How that specific portion is punctuated and whether its grammar follows conventions
What the main idea of the entire passage is, apart from this specific portion
Which word in that specific portion has the most complex meaning in the context
What that specific portion accomplishes in the passage (e.g., transition, emphasis, support)
quiz.e: Function questions test what role a sentence/paragraph plays in the passage's structure or argument, not just its content.

quiz.q: What does a Reading 'sequence of events' question ask you to determine?
o: The emotional shift in the narrator's attitude across the passage's paragraphs
The chronological or logical order in which events occurred in the passage
The reasons the author gives for choosing to write about these events
The relationship between two characters described in the opening paragraph
quiz.e: Sequence questions test whether you can track the order of events as presented or implied in the text.

quiz.q: Which best describes the pattern of a Math question that provides a table of x and y values?
o: Average all of the listed x and y values to find a typical pair
Round every value in the table to the nearest whole number first
Find the largest y value and match it to the closest answer choice
Identify the underlying rule or relationship connecting x and y
quiz.e: These questions test your ability to spot a pattern (e.g., linear, quadratic) linking the given values.

quiz.q: What is the trap in an ACT inequality question that catches many students?
o: Forgetting to flip the inequality sign when multiplying or dividing by a negative number
Flipping the inequality sign when adding or subtracting a negative number on both sides
Dividing both sides by a positive number and keeping the inequality sign the same
Adding the same positive number to both sides and changing the direction of the sign
quiz.e: Multiplying or dividing both sides of an inequality by a negative number requires flipping the inequality's direction.

quiz.q: What does an ACT Reading 'comparison' question on a paired-passage set typically ask?
o: Which passage uses more precise and descriptive language on a shared topic
What each passage's grammar conventions reveal about the era of the writing
How the two passages relate to or differ from each other on a shared topic
Which passage's conclusion the student personally agrees with more strongly
quiz.e: Comparison questions test your grasp of both passages' viewpoints on the same topic and how they relate.

quiz.q: What is the best way to handle a long, dense sentence during a first read of a Reading passage?
o: Pause and rewrite the sentence in your own words before moving on to the next
Get the gist and keep moving, returning only if a question requires precise detail
Underline every word you cannot define and look for its meaning in the choices
Skip the rest of the paragraph and rely on the question stems to explain it
quiz.e: Efficient first reads prioritize overall understanding; dense sentences can be revisited only if a specific question demands it.

quiz.q: On ACT Science, what should you check first when comparing data across multiple similar graphs?
o: The overall shape of each line, since similar shapes mean similar data
The axis labels and scales, since they can differ between graphs
The legend colors alone, since matching colors signal identical variables
The number of data points plotted, since more points mean greater accuracy
quiz.e: Graphs that look similar can have different axis scales, which changes what the data actually shows.

quiz.q: What is the risk of two graphs using different y-axis scales (one 0-10, one 0-1000)?
o: Concluding the graph with the smaller axis range must show an invalid experiment
Misreading similar-looking trends as equivalent in magnitude when they aren't
Believing the scale difference changes the data values listed in the passage
Thinking two graphs can't both show the same variable on their horizontal axes
quiz.e: Different scales can make trends look visually similar even though the actual magnitudes differ greatly.

quiz.q: What is the pattern behind a 'least supported' Reading question?
o: Find the answer choice that is quoted most closely from the passage, unlike the others which are paraphrases
Find the answer choice with the strongest textual evidence backing it, unlike the others which are weaker
Find the answer choice that states the passage's main idea, unlike the others which cover only minor details
Find the answer choice with the weakest textual evidence backing it, unlike the others which are well supported
quiz.e: 'Least supported' questions invert the usual task — you're looking for the choice evidence supports least well.

quiz.q: What is a common wrong-answer trap on ACT Reading questions?
o: An answer that paraphrases a sentence from the passage and matches its overall meaning
An answer that is true in general but not actually stated or supported in this passage
An answer that cites a specific line of the passage and explains the author's reasoning
An answer that addresses the exact question asked and stays within the passage's scope
quiz.e: Reading traps often include statements that are plausible or generally true but not supported by this specific passage.

quiz.q: What does a Science question asking you to identify a flaw in an experiment's design usually test?
o: Whether you can spot a missing control or uncontrolled variable
Whether you know the exact chemical formulas involved
Whether you can count the number of trials only
Whether you memorized the scientists' names
quiz.e: Experimental-flaw questions typically hinge on identifying a missing control group or an unaccounted-for variable.

quiz.q: What pattern should guide combining information from two related Science experiments?
o: Average the results from both experiments to find a single combined value
Identify what changed between the experiments and what stayed the same
Assume the conditions of the second experiment match those of the first
Focus on the experiment with more trials and disregard the other's data
quiz.e: Multi-experiment questions often hinge on comparing what variable changed versus what was held constant.

quiz.q: What is the pattern in ACT English questions asking about combining two short, choppy sentences?
o: Look for the option that joins them logically and concisely, often with a conjunction or subordination
Look for the option that keeps them as separate sentences and adds transitional words at the start
Look for the option that joins them with a comma alone, since it keeps the original wording intact
Look for the option that joins them with the most descriptive phrasing, often with added modifiers
quiz.e: Combining-sentence questions reward a logical, concise join — often via a conjunction, semicolon, or subordinate clause.

quiz.q: On ACT English, what is the pattern behind a question asking whether a sentence should be 'kept' or 'deleted'?
o: Whether the sentence adds relevant, non-redundant information supporting the passage's purpose
Whether the sentence has an interesting detail even if it strays from the paragraph's focus
Whether the sentence repeats the main point of the paragraph in slightly different words
Whether the sentence is written in the same tone as the sentences placed around it
quiz.e: Keep/delete questions test relevance and non-redundancy, not just grammatical correctness.

quiz.q: What is the recognizable pattern of a 'main idea' Reading question with two seemingly plausible choices?
o: The correct answer captures the passage's central focus, not just one supported detail
The correct answer focuses on the most vivid detail the passage describes in depth
The correct answer is the narrower of the two since specific claims are safer ones
The correct answer repeats the passage's opening sentence in slightly different words
quiz.e: A true main-idea answer reflects the passage's overall focus, while a trap choice may reflect only a specific detail.

quiz.q: What does the ACT Science pattern of 'supported by data' require for a hypothesis?
o: The data must include the exact numbers named in the hypothesis's wording
The data trend must align with and not contradict the hypothesis's claim
The data must prove the hypothesis true at every individual value listed
The hypothesis must come from the scientist who also gathered the data
quiz.e: A hypothesis is 'supported' when the data trend is consistent with, not contradicting, its claim.

quiz.q: What pattern helps identify the dependent variable in an experiment?
o: It's the factor the scientist deliberately changes to see how the outcome responds
It's the condition kept the same across all trials to ensure a fair comparison
It's the control group that receives no treatment in the experiment's design
It's the outcome measured, which changes in response to the manipulated variable
quiz.e: The dependent variable is the measured outcome that responds to changes in the independent variable.

quiz.q: What is the recognizable ACT Math pattern for testing algebra questions with answer choices?
o: Solve the equation using the most complicated method to guard against mistakes
Eliminate the choices with fractions since the correct value is a whole number
Pick the choice closest to the number that appears most in the problem statement
Plug the answer choices back into the original equation to see which one works
quiz.e: Backsolving — plugging answer choices into the equation — is often the fastest path on multiple-choice algebra questions.

quiz.q: What is the common pattern tested by ACT English idiomatic-preposition questions?
o: Choosing the preposition that conventionally pairs with a specific word, even if others seem plausible
Choosing the preposition that sounds most natural in context, even if it is not conventional
Choosing the preposition that matches the one used earlier in the sentence, even if another fits
Choosing the longest prepositional phrase that sounds formal, even if the shorter one is idiomatic
quiz.e: Idiom questions test fixed word-preposition pairings that must match conventional usage, not the 'most correct'-sounding option.

quiz.q: What is the tested pattern behind an ACT Reading 'function' vs. 'main idea' distinction?
o: Function asks what the whole passage is about; main idea asks what one part *does* in the passage
Function asks about the author's word choice; main idea asks about the passage's tone overall
Function asks for a detail stated in the text; main idea asks for an inference about it
Function asks what a part *does* in the passage; main idea asks what the *whole* passage is about
quiz.e: Function questions target the role of a specific part, while main idea questions target the passage as a whole.

quiz.q: What pattern should guide a question that asks which experimental trial had the highest reaction rate?
o: Locate and directly compare the specific data values across trials in the given table or graph
Estimate which trial changed most from the first, using the passage's general description alone
Find the trial listed with the most variables adjusted and assume it has the highest rate
Calculate the average rate across all trials and pick the trial closest to that average
quiz.e: This is a direct data-lookup pattern — compare the actual reported values across trials.

quiz.q: What is the pattern behind a Reading question asking about the narrator's attitude toward something?
o: Count how many sentences the narrator devotes to that subject in the passage
Look for word choice and tone cues the author uses when describing that subject
Use the plot outcome at the end to decide how the narrator must have felt
Rely on the opinions that the other characters express aloud about that subject
quiz.e: Attitude questions hinge on diction and tone the author uses, not just plot facts.

quiz.q: What is the tested pattern in an ACT English question about correcting a dangling modifier?
o: The modifier must be moved to the end of the sentence away from the subject
The modifier must be placed after the verb so that it describes the action
The subject performing the modifier's action must appear right after it
The modifier must be separated from the sentence by a semicolon at its end
quiz.e: A modifier must clearly attach to the subject performing that action, which should immediately follow it.

quiz.q: What is the primary purpose of taking full-length, timed ACT practice tests?
o: To build stamina and get an accurate score estimate under real conditions
To learn the actual questions so they can be answered quickly on test day
To replace all content review with repeated exposure to the test format
To earn a guaranteed score improvement for each additional test completed
quiz.e: Full-length timed tests simulate real conditions, building stamina and giving an accurate baseline score.

quiz.q: What is an error log used for in ACT prep?
o: Recording the time of day each practice test was taken to find your best hour
Listing every vocabulary word encountered so that you can memorize each one
Keeping a count of the questions answered correctly to compute your composite
Tracking every missed question by category to reveal patterns of weakness
quiz.e: An error log organizes mistakes by category (e.g., comma usage, inference) so patterns of weakness become clear.

quiz.q: When is the best time to review a missed question from a practice test?
o: After a full week, once your frustration about the score has faded
Immediately before the next test so that the mistakes stay in mind
Within 24 hours, while your reasoning process is still fresh
Only after taking the real exam, when you know which topics appeared
quiz.e: Reviewing soon after the test — while your thought process is still fresh — makes it easier to diagnose exactly what went wrong.

quiz.q: What does 'simulating test-day conditions' during practice involve?
o: Taking each section whenever convenient and checking messages between them
Matching wake time, breaks, and a no-phone rule to the real test day
Practicing in a relaxed setting with music and extra time on every section
Taking sections in a random order with unlimited breaks and no time limit
quiz.e: Matching real test-day conditions during practice reduces surprises and builds familiarity with the actual experience.

quiz.q: What is the fixed order of ACT sections on test day?
o: Math, English, Science, Reading, then optional Writing
English, Reading, Math, Science, then optional Writing
Writing, English, Math, Reading, then optional Science
English, Math, Reading, Science, then optional Writing
quiz.e: The ACT always follows the order English, Math, Reading, Science, with the optional Writing test last.

quiz.q: Why is target-score planning useful in ACT prep?
o: It determines which colleges will accept your scores regardless of the result
It shows which sections need the most improvement to reach a composite goal
It sets the number of questions the ACT will count toward your final score
It tells you which test date will have the easiest questions for your goal
quiz.e: Calculating needed section gains toward a composite goal helps prioritize study time efficiently.

quiz.q: How often should full-length practice tests generally be scheduled?
o: Roughly every 1-2 weeks, with review time in between
Roughly every 2-3 days, with only a short break between
Roughly once a month, with no review done in between
Roughly every weekend until the real test, skipping all review
quiz.e: Spacing practice tests out, with time to review and apply lessons, is more effective than cramming them back-to-back.

quiz.q: What should a post-test pacing analysis focus on?
o: Replacing the timing plan for every section whenever the composite score declines
Identifying which section ran out of time and adjusting that section's pacing plan
Determining which section had the most questions and shortening its time limit
Measuring how long the breaks lasted and adjusting the schedule between sections
quiz.e: Pacing analysis pinpoints exactly which section needs pacing adjustments based on where time ran out.

quiz.q: Why are official, retired ACT tests recommended for practice?
o: They are guaranteed to contain questions repeated on the real exam
They cost less than commercial prep books and score more quickly
They include extra hints that reveal how to approach each question type
They most accurately reflect real question style and difficulty
quiz.e: Official retired tests are written by the same test maker, making them the most reliable practice material.

quiz.q: What should a student do differently in the final week before the real ACT?
o: Increase full practice tests to daily and focus on exhausting every weak area
Study new advanced content late into the night to cover any remaining gaps
Taper full practice tests and focus on light review and confidence-building
Stop all review and avoid ACT materials from the first day of the week
quiz.e: A final-week taper avoids burnout and keeps focus on reinforcing existing strengths rather than cramming new material.

quiz.q: What is the value of comparing error logs across multiple practice tests over time?
o: It shows which test form contained the easiest questions across the set
It proves that your scores will continue to rise at a steady rate
It indicates which sections the ACT is likely to weigh more heavily
It reveals whether previously weak categories are actually improving
quiz.e: Tracking error categories over multiple tests shows whether targeted practice is actually closing gaps.

quiz.q: What is a common mistake when reviewing a missed practice question?
o: Writing down the type of error you made and the rule you should have applied
Just noting the correct answer without understanding why your reasoning went wrong
Redoing the problem on a blank page to see where your first attempt diverged
Rereading the passage or problem before checking the explanation for the first time
quiz.e: Simply memorizing the right answer, without diagnosing the reasoning error, doesn't fix the underlying skill gap.

quiz.q: Why is it useful to take at least one practice test in an unfamiliar, less comfortable environment?
o: It guarantees the real test will be held in comfortable familiar surroundings
It raises your score automatically because stress improves recall and focus
It helps prepare for possible distractions or discomfort on actual test day
It replaces full-length timed tests since the environment matters most
quiz.e: Practicing under less-than-ideal conditions builds resilience against distractions that might occur on the real test day.

quiz.q: What should a student prioritize if their error log shows most mistakes cluster in one section?
o: Extra targeted practice specifically in that weak section
Ignoring that section since it's a lost cause
Spending equal time on all sections regardless of the data
Retaking only full tests with no section-specific drills
quiz.e: An error log pointing to a specific weak section calls for focused practice on exactly that area.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of reviewing not just wrong answers, but also correct guesses on practice tests?
o: It confirms that every correct answer reflects mastery, so those topics can be dropped
It shows which questions the test writers considered easiest, so you can skip them later
It reveals which questions you answered fastest, which guarantees success on similar ones
It reveals answers you got right without solid reasoning, which may fail on harder questions
quiz.e: A correct guess without solid reasoning is a hidden weak spot that harder or differently worded questions could expose.

quiz.q: Why match your practice test's start time to your actual scheduled test time?
o: It trains your focus and energy levels to peak at the same time of day as the real test
It changes the difficulty of the questions to match the time you tend to be alert
It allows the testing agency to adjust your section timing to your body clock
It guarantees you will feel rested regardless of how much sleep you actually get
quiz.e: Aligning practice and real test times helps your energy and focus naturally peak when it counts.

quiz.q: What role does a rest/sleep routine play in full practice-test workflow?
o: Sleep schedules matter only on the night before the real exam, not during practice-test weeks
Consistent sleep before both practice and real tests supports accurate performance data and readiness
Staying up late before practice tests builds tolerance to fatigue for the real test day
Sleep affects only the essay section, so the multiple-choice practice can be done tired
quiz.e: Consistent sleep habits during practice give a truer read on performance and build the same routine for test day.

quiz.q: If a student's composite score plateaus despite regular full practice tests, what should change?
o: The test date — postponing the exam until scores rise without changing how they study
The type of review — targeting specific error patterns rather than just repeating full tests
The difficulty of practice — switching to easier tests to build confidence and raise scores
The number of sections — focusing on a single subject and ignoring the composite goal
quiz.e: A plateau usually means the practice-test volume is fine but the review process needs to become more targeted.

quiz.q: Why keep practice-test conditions consistent (same room, same rules) across multiple practice sessions?
o: It causes the ACT to apply the same curve to each of your results
It makes the practice questions become easier each time you retake them
It lets you skip reviewing wrong answers since conditions stay the same
It makes score comparisons across tests more meaningful and reliable
quiz.e: Comparable conditions across tests make it easier to trust that score changes reflect actual improvement.

quiz.q: What is a smart way to use a practice test's score report beyond just the composite score?
o: Break down performance by section and question category to guide the next study cycle
Compare your composite score only against the national average to set your next goal
Rely on the highest section score to choose which subject to study the next cycle
