Check the date and time listed on the report to pick the next practice session
quiz.e: A detailed breakdown by section and category gives far more actionable guidance than the composite alone.

quiz.q: Why is it important to time each section separately during a full practice test rather than using one combined clock?
o: Each ACT section has its own strict, separate time limit on the real test
The real test gives one total time block that students may divide as needed
Combined timing would let unused minutes carry into later sections of the test
Only the Math and Science sections are timed separately on the real exam
quiz.e: Matching the real test's separate section clocks makes practice-test pacing data accurate and transferable.

quiz.q: What is the benefit of debriefing a practice test with a tutor, teacher, or study partner?
o: A second perspective can catch reasoning errors you might miss reviewing alone
A tutor can predict your exact composite score and determine your target date
A study partner can supply the real answers to questions from upcoming tests
Another person's opinion removes the need to track time or record mistakes
quiz.e: An outside perspective can spot patterns or reasoning gaps that self-review alone might overlook.

quiz.q: How should a full practice-test schedule change as test day approaches?
o: More full tests as the date nears, with the highest number in the final week
Fewer full tests and more focused review as the date nears, tapering off in the final week
The same schedule throughout, with a full test in every week including the last
Only light review early on, then a series of full tests during the final week
quiz.e: A taper toward the end avoids burnout and channels energy into review rather than fatigue-inducing repetition.

quiz.q: What should a student do if a practice test reveals a section score drop compared to a previous test?
o: Treat it as proof that the most recent study methods failed and switch to entirely new ones at once
Assume it was caused by test difficulty and keep the same plan without any further investigation
Investigate whether it reflects a content gap, timing issue, or an off day, then adjust the study plan
Retake the same practice test the next day to restore the score before changing anything else
quiz.e: A single lower score needs investigation — it could be content, timing, fatigue, or simple variance — before changing the plan.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of setting a specific target composite score before starting a full practice-test cycle?
o: It determines which sections will be scored on the real test and which are removed
It gives a concrete benchmark to measure progress and guide section-level priorities
It tells the testing agency which scores to report to your chosen colleges first
It fixes the number of practice tests that must be completed before registering
quiz.e: A target score provides a clear benchmark against which practice-test results and study priorities can be measured.

quiz.q: Why review both the questions you got wrong AND the reasoning behind questions you got right by luck?
o: To confirm that lucky guesses count toward your score the same as reasoned answers
To ensure your process, not just the outcome, is actually reliable for future questions
To collect additional correct answers to add to the error log's total of strengths
To check whether each correct answer matches the number of minutes you spent on it
quiz.e: A sound process is what generalizes to new questions — a lucky guess doesn't guarantee future success.

quiz.q: What is a reasonable full practice-test cadence in the final month before the real ACT?
o: One full test every 1-2 weeks, tapering in the very last week
Five full tests every single day
One single full test months in advance and none after
Full tests only after the real exam has already happened
quiz.e: A steady, spaced cadence with a final taper balances realistic practice against burnout risk.

quiz.q: Why should error-log categories be specific (e.g., 'comma splices') rather than vague (e.g., 'grammar')?
o: Specific categories make the log shorter, while vague ones need extra time to maintain
Specific categories are scored by the ACT, while vague ones are ignored in reports
Specific categories reveal strengths, while vague ones mainly show your weak areas
Specific categories point directly to what to practice next; vague ones don't guide action
quiz.e: A specific category like 'comma splices' tells you exactly what skill to drill, while 'grammar' is too broad to act on.

quiz.q: What should a full practice-test debrief include besides the raw score?
o: Your confidence rating for each section, the room used, and the date taken
Time spent per section, error categories, and specific missed-question review
The composite score, a list of the passages read, and the test proctor's notes
Total study hours, the score goal, and your friends' scores on the same test
quiz.e: A thorough debrief covers pacing data and specific error patterns, not just the final score.

quiz.q: Why might taking a practice test without any breaks (matching real ACT breaks) give a misleading result?
o: It makes the test shorter than the real one and so inflates the section difficulty
It doesn't accurately simulate the fatigue pattern of the actual multi-section test day
It changes the question order, so the Math section no longer follows English
It removes the time limits from the sections so the pacing cannot be measured
quiz.e: Matching the real test's break structure gives a more accurate simulation of fatigue and pacing across sections.

quiz.q: What is the risk of only ever taking practice tests and never doing focused skill drills?
o: The error log becomes inaccurate when the full tests are taken too frequently
Full tests become harder over time, which produces lower and lower scores
Weak areas identified by the error log may never get isolated, targeted practice
The scoring on practice tests becomes unreliable without drills as a baseline
quiz.e: Full tests reveal weaknesses, but isolated skill drills are often needed to actually fix them.

quiz.q: Why is it useful to note not just which questions were missed, but also which were answered slowly?
o: Slow answers show which topics are the most difficult for the average test taker
Slow answers are likely to be marked incorrect when scored on the real exam
Slow answers prove the content has been mastered and needs no further practice
Slow-but-correct answers reveal pacing risks even where the content skill is solid
quiz.e: A correct but slow answer signals a pacing risk that could cause problems on a timed real test even without a content gap.

quiz.q: What is a good way to translate error-log findings into a weekly study plan?
o: Divide study sessions evenly across categories, no matter how often errors occur
Allocate specific study sessions to the highest-frequency error categories
Schedule sessions only for the categories where you made the fewest mistakes
Assign study sessions based on how interesting each category feels to you
quiz.e: Prioritizing the most frequent error categories makes study time proportional to actual need.

quiz.q: What is a downside of taking full practice tests too close together with no time to review?
o: The tests become too easy, so the scores no longer reflect the real exam's difficulty
The testing agency flags frequent attempts and may delay your official score report
Lessons from one test aren't applied before the next, reducing the value of practice
The questions begin to repeat across forms, which inflates the practice test scores
quiz.e: Without review time between tests, mistakes tend to repeat instead of being corrected.

quiz.q: How does a full practice-test workflow support building test-day confidence?
o: Familiarity with pacing, format, and question types reduces surprises and anxiety
Confidence is unrelated to how much practice a student has done
Only content knowledge affects confidence, not practice format
Practice tests typically increase anxiety with no benefit
quiz.e: Repeated exposure to the real format and pacing builds familiarity that reduces test-day anxiety.

quiz.q: What is the best response if a full practice test score is lower than expected right before the real test?
o: Review calmly for likely causes (fatigue, timing, content) without panicking or over-correcting
Overhaul the entire study plan immediately, focusing on the weakest section until test day
Treat the score as the likely outcome and lower the target composite to match the result
Take the same practice test again the next day to verify whether the low score was real
quiz.e: A single low score close to test day should be diagnosed calmly, not treated as a certain predictor or a reason to over-cram.

quiz.q: Why is reviewing the explanation for a correctly answered question sometimes still worthwhile?
o: It allows you to count the question as mastered and remove it from later review
It reveals which answers were easiest so they can be removed from your error log
It can reveal a flawed reasoning process that happened to reach the right answer
It shows how the question writers decided which choices would be marked as right
quiz.e: Even a correct answer benefits from a reasoning check, since flawed logic can produce the right answer by chance.

quiz.q: Why should a student track total time spent studying, not just test scores, in their practice workflow?
o: It helps estimate the exact composite score you will receive on test day from your hours
It helps evaluate whether study methods are efficient, not just whether scores are improving
It lets you prove to the testing agency that you completed the required preparation
It shows whether you studied for long enough to make additional practice tests unnecessary
quiz.e: Comparing time invested to score gains helps identify whether study methods are actually efficient.

quiz.q: What is a good way to incorporate content review (grammar rules, math formulas) into a full practice-test workflow?
o: Alternate practice tests with dedicated content-review sessions based on the error log
Do all content review in one session at the start and then take only practice tests
Review content only the night before each practice test using a general study guide
Replace practice tests with content review once your composite reaches an average score
quiz.e: Alternating full tests with targeted content review, guided by the error log, closes gaps more effectively than either alone.

quiz.q: Why is consistency in how a student marks 'uncertain' answers useful across practice tests?
o: It allows the scorer to give partial credit for answers that were marked uncertain
It shows which questions the test makers labeled uncertain in the answer explanations
It creates a reliable way to identify true guesses versus confident wrong answers during review
It ensures all marked answers are reviewed last so the confident ones are checked first
quiz.e: A consistent way to flag guesses lets review focus on the answers where reasoning actually broke down.

quiz.q: Which sentence contains a comma splice?
o: The storm ended, and the sun came out.
The storm ended, the sun came out.
The storm ended; the sun came out.
After the storm ended, the sun came out.
quiz.e: Two independent clauses joined only by a comma (no conjunction) is a comma splice.

quiz.q: Choose the best revision: 'The committee, that reviewed the budget, approved it.'
o: The committee, that reviewed the budget approved it.
The committee that reviewed the budget approved it.
The committee that reviewed the budget, approved it.
The committee, that reviewed the budget approved, it.
quiz.e: 'That reviewed the budget' is a restrictive (essential) clause and takes no commas.

quiz.q: Which is the correct way to join two independent clauses with a semicolon?
o: I studied hard; and I passed.
I studied hard; I passed.
I studied hard, I passed;
I studied hard; because I passed.
quiz.e: A semicolon alone (no conjunction) can join two independent clauses.

quiz.q: 'The recipe calls for: eggs, flour, and milk.' What's wrong?
o: A colon should never follow a verb like 'calls for'.
A comma should be added after the word 'recipe'.
'Eggs' should be capitalized because it follows a colon.
The word 'and' should be removed from the list.
quiz.e: A colon must follow a complete independent clause, not a verb or preposition.

quiz.q: Which sentence uses a dash correctly to set off nonessential information?
o: The trip—despite the rain, was fun.
The trip, despite the rain—was fun.
The trip—despite the rain—was fun.
The trip despite the rain—was fun.
quiz.e: Dashes used to set off a nonessential phrase must appear in a matching pair, like parentheses.

quiz.q: Identify the subject-verb agreement error: 'The list of items are on the table.'
o: 'are' should be 'is' because the subject is the singular 'list'
'list' should be 'lists' because there are several items in the list
'items' should be 'item' because the verb needs a singular subject
'table' should be 'tables' to agree with the plural noun 'items'
quiz.e: The subject is 'list' (singular), not the object of the prepositional phrase 'of items', so the verb must be 'is'.

quiz.q: Which pronoun correctly completes: 'Each of the students turned in ___ essay.'
o: their
his or her
they're
our
quiz.e: 'Each' is singular, so it requires a singular pronoun; 'his or her' agrees in number.

quiz.q: Choose the correctly punctuated sentence.
o: My favorite subjects are: math, science, and art.
My favorite subjects are math, science, and art.
My favorite subjects, are math, science, and art.
My favorite subjects are; math, science, and art.
quiz.e: No punctuation is needed before a list that directly completes the sentence (predicate).

quiz.q: On the ACT English test, when is 'NO CHANGE' most likely correct?
o: When the underlined portion is the longest of the options and adds the most detail
When the underlined portion sounds natural when read aloud, even if it contains a minor error
When the underlined portion is already grammatically correct and stylistically appropriate
When two of the other options appear to be identical in meaning and construction
quiz.e: NO CHANGE is correct roughly a quarter of the time and should be picked whenever the original is correct and concise.

quiz.q: Which revision fixes a misplaced modifier? 'Running to catch the bus, the coffee spilled on my shirt.'
o: Running to catch the bus, my shirt got coffee spilled on it.
While running to catch the bus, I spilled coffee on my shirt.
The coffee, running to catch the bus, spilled on my shirt.
Running to catch the bus, my coffee spilled on my shirt.
quiz.e: The introductory phrase must modify the subject that is actually doing the running—'I', not the coffee.

quiz.q: Which sentence uses parallel structure correctly?
o: She likes hiking, to swim, and biking.
She likes hiking, swimming, and biking.
She likes to hike, swimming, and to bike.
She likes hiking, swim, and to bike.
quiz.e: All items in a list/series must share the same grammatical form—here, all gerunds.

quiz.q: Choose the most concise revision of: 'Due to the fact that it was raining, we stayed inside.'
o: Due to the fact it was raining, we stayed inside.
Because it was raining, we stayed inside.
Because of the fact that it was raining, we stayed inside.
On account of it raining, we stayed inside.
quiz.e: The ACT rewards concision; 'because' replaces the wordy phrase 'due to the fact that' with no loss of meaning.

quiz.q: A 'writer's goal' question asks whether adding a sentence achieves a stated purpose. What should guide your answer?
o: Whether the sentence is the most elegant and well written option available
Whether the sentence specifically accomplishes the stated goal in the question
Whether the sentence adds the greatest amount of vivid detail to the paragraph
Whether the sentence is the shortest way of expressing a related idea clearly
quiz.e: These questions are graded strictly against the stated goal, not general writing quality.

quiz.q: Which transition word correctly shows contrast?
o: Furthermore
However
Therefore
Similarly
quiz.e: 'However' signals contrast; the other options signal addition, result, or similarity.

quiz.q: Identify the correct verb tense: 'By the time the movie started, we ___ our seats.'
o: find
have found
had found
are finding
quiz.e: Past perfect ('had found') is needed because finding the seats happened before another past action (the movie starting).

quiz.q: Which sentence correctly uses 'who' vs. 'whom'?
o: Who did you give the book to?
Whom did you give the book to?
Whom gave you the book?
Who's book did you give?
quiz.e: 'Whom' is the object of the preposition 'to', so the objective case is correct.

quiz.q: Which option best fixes a redundancy? 'She returned back to the store to buy a new pair of shoes.'
o: She returned back to the store.
She returned to the store.
She went back returning to the store.
She returned back again to the store.
quiz.e: 'Returned back' is redundant since 'return' already means 'go back'.

quiz.q: Which sentence correctly places the modifier 'only'?
o: She only ate vegetables for dinner.
Only she ate vegetables for dinner.
She ate only vegetables for dinner.
She ate vegetables only for dinner.
quiz.e: 'Only' should sit directly before the word or phrase it limits—here, 'vegetables'.

quiz.q: In a paragraph reordering question, what's the best strategy?
o: Place the sentence with the most vivid detail first to grab the reader
Keep the order that has the fewest changes from the original sequence
Arrange the sentences by length so that the shortest ones come first
Use transition words and pronoun references to trace logical sequence
quiz.e: Transitions and pronouns reveal which sentence must follow which, showing the logical chain.

quiz.q: Which choice avoids a dangling modifier? 'Having finished the exam early, ___'
o: the room felt quiet to Maria.
it was quiet when Maria left the room.
Maria left the room quietly.
the room was left quietly by Maria.
quiz.e: The subject after the modifier must be the one who finished the exam—Maria.

quiz.q: Which is the correct possessive form: 'The ___ decision affected everyone.'
o: committees
committee's
committees'
committee's'
quiz.e: A singular committee acting as one body takes a simple apostrophe-s for possession.

quiz.q: Choose the sentence with correct apostrophe use for a plural possessive.
o: The dog's bones were buried in the yard.
The dogs' bones were buried in the yard.
The dogs's bones were buried in the yard.
The dog's bone's were buried in the yard.
quiz.e: For a plural noun ending in 's' (dogs), the possessive apostrophe goes after the 's'.

quiz.q: Which sentence corrects a run-on?
o: I love reading books I read every night.
I love reading books, I read every night.
I love reading books; I read every night.
I love reading books because I read every night I love reading.
quiz.e: A semicolon correctly joins the two independent clauses without a conjunction.

quiz.q: A question asks you to 'add a sentence that emphasizes the historical significance of the event.' Which type of ACT question is this?
o: Usage and mechanics (verb agreement)
Sentence structure (clause boundaries)
Conventions of punctuation (commas)
Rhetorical skills (writer's purpose)
quiz.e: This tests rhetorical skills—whether an addition accomplishes a specific stated purpose, not grammar.

quiz.q: Which revision uses the correct idiomatic preposition? 'She is capable ___ solving the problem.'
o: for
of
in
at
quiz.e: The correct idiom is 'capable of,' not 'capable for/in/at'.

quiz.q: Which choice correctly uses a comma with a coordinating conjunction joining two independent clauses?
o: I wanted to go, but I stayed home.
I wanted to go but, I stayed home.
I wanted to go but I stayed, home.
I wanted, to go but I stayed home.
quiz.e: A comma belongs before the coordinating conjunction (but) when it joins two independent clauses.

quiz.q: Which sentence avoids an unnecessary shift in verb tense?
o: She walks to school and arrived early.
She walked to school and arrives early.
She walked to school and arrived early.
She walk to school and arrived early.
quiz.e: Both verbs should stay in the same past tense for consistency.

quiz.q: Choose the best word for precision: 'The experiment had a big ___ on the results.'
o: affect
effect
effected
affects
quiz.e: 'Effect' is the noun meaning result/impact; 'affect' is normally the verb.

quiz.q: Which choice correctly uses 'fewer' vs. 'less'?
o: fewer traffic
fewer cars
less cars
less amount of cars
quiz.e: 'Fewer' is used with countable nouns like 'cars'; 'less' is for uncountable quantities.

quiz.q: A passage ends and asks 'which choice best concludes the essay by returning to its opening idea?' What should you check first?
o: The most elaborate vocabulary choice
The essay's opening sentence or idea
The shortest available option
Whichever choice mentions the author
quiz.e: 'Returning to the opening idea' questions require comparing options against the introduction's content.

quiz.q: Which is grammatically correct?
o: Between you and I, the plan will work.
Between you and me, the plan will work.
Between you and myself, the plan will work.
Between I and you, the plan will work.
quiz.e: 'Between' is a preposition and takes the objective case 'me,' not 'I'.

quiz.q: Which sentence correctly uses 'its' vs. 'it's'?
o: Its going to rain today.
The dog wagged it's tail.
The company changed its policy.
The company changed it's policy.
quiz.e: 'Its' is the possessive form; 'it's' is a contraction of 'it is'.

quiz.q: Which revision eliminates wordiness? 'In today's modern society of today, technology is everywhere.'
o: In today's modern society, technology is everywhere.
Today, technology is everywhere.
In today's society of today, technology is everywhere.
In modern society today, technology is everywhere.
quiz.e: 'Today' alone conveys the same meaning without the redundant phrase 'modern society of today'.

quiz.q: Which choice is best when a question asks you to combine two short, choppy sentences?
o: Combine them with a comma alone so the sentences keep their original wording exactly.
Combine them by adding the longest descriptive phrase that links their separate topics.
Combine them using a relevant conjunction or subordinate clause that shows their relationship.
Keep them separate and add a transitional phrase of several words to each beginning.
quiz.e: Effective combination should reflect the logical relationship (cause, contrast, sequence) between the ideas.

quiz.q: Which sentence uses the correct relative pronoun for a person?
o: The teacher which helped me is retiring.
The teacher who helped me is retiring.
The teacher whom helped me is retiring.
The teacher that whom helped me is retiring.
quiz.e: 'Who' is used for people as the subject of the clause; 'which' refers to things.

quiz.q: In an ACT passage, a question asks if a sentence should be 'kept' or 'deleted.' What determines the answer?
o: Whether the sentence is written in a more formal tone than those around it
Whether the sentence is interesting enough to hold the reader's attention
Whether the sentence repeats an earlier point so the main idea is emphasized
Whether the sentence adds relevant information that supports the passage's focus
quiz.e: Keep/delete questions hinge on relevance to the passage's purpose and focus, not just grammar.

quiz.q: Which choice avoids redundancy? 'He is a man who is honest and truthful and doesn't lie.'
o: He is a man who is honest and truthful.
He is honest.
He is a truthful man who doesn't lie and is honest.
He is a man who is honest, truthful, and doesn't lie.
quiz.e: 'Honest,' 'truthful,' and 'doesn't lie' all repeat the same idea; the ACT rewards the most concise accurate version.

quiz.q: Which sentence correctly uses a colon?
o: She had one goal: to win the championship.
She had one goal, to: win the championship.
Her goal was to: win the championship.
She had: one goal, to win the championship.
quiz.e: The colon follows a complete independent clause ('She had one goal') and introduces an explanation.

quiz.q: Which is the best way to fix a vague pronoun reference? 'When Sam met Jake, he was nervous.'
o: When Sam met Jake, he was nervous, really.
When Sam met Jake, Sam was nervous.
When Sam met Jake, they were nervous.
When meeting, he was nervous.
quiz.e: Naming 'Sam' directly removes the ambiguity of what 'he' refers to.

quiz.q: Which choice correctly uses the idiom 'different from'?
o: This is different than that.
This is different to that.
This is different from that.
This is differently from that.
quiz.e: Standard written English idiom is 'different from,' which the ACT tests directly.

quiz.q: Solve for x: 3x + 7 = 22
What is the slope of the line through (2,3) and (6,11)?
If f(x) = 2x^2 - 3, what is f(-2)?
What is the area of a circle with radius 6?
o: 6π
quiz.e: Area = πr^2 = π(36) = 36π.

quiz.q: Simplify: (x^3)(x^5)
quiz.e: When multiplying like bases, add the exponents: x^(3+5)=x^8.

quiz.q: A right triangle has legs 6 and 8. What is the hypotenuse?
quiz.e: By the Pythagorean theorem, sqrt(6^2+8^2)=sqrt(100)=10.

quiz.q: Solve the system: y = 2x + 1 and y = x + 4.
quiz.e: Setting equal: 2x+1=x+4 → x=3, then y=2(3)+1=7.

quiz.q: What is 15% of 240?
Which strategy is fastest for a question that says 'for all values of x' with variables in the answer choices?
o: Solving the equation for x using full algebra first
Picking the choice that contains the most variable terms
Expanding every choice by hand and comparing all coefficients
Plugging in a smart number for x and testing choices
quiz.e: Plugging in numbers (avoiding 0 and 1) quickly eliminates wrong answer choices for variable expressions.

quiz.q: If sin(θ) = 3/5 in a right triangle, what is cos(θ) (acute angle)?
quiz.e: With opposite=3, hypotenuse=5, adjacent=4 (3-4-5 triangle), so cos(θ)=4/5.

quiz.q: What is the value of x in log₂(x) = 5?
Factor: x^2 - 9
quiz.e: Difference of squares: x^2-9=(x-3)(x+3).

quiz.q: A bag has 4 red and 6 blue marbles. What is the probability of drawing a red marble?
quiz.e: P(red) = 4 red / 10 total = 4/10 = 2/5.

quiz.q: What is the median of the set {3, 7, 9, 12, 20}?
quiz.e: With 5 numbers sorted, the median is the middle (3rd) value: 9.

quiz.q: Simplify: 2/3 + 1/4
quiz.e: Common denominator 12: 8/12 + 3/12 = 11/12.

quiz.q: Which is the fastest way to solve a multiple-choice algebra question by testing answer choices?
o: Solving the full equation algebraically from scratch and then checking it against the choices
Starting with the largest answer choice and working downward through every choice in order
Estimating the answer by rounding the numbers and choosing the choice that looks closest
Backsolving by plugging answer choices into the original equation, starting with a middle value
quiz.e: Backsolving from a middle answer choice narrows down whether to try a larger or smaller value next, often faster than full algebra.

quiz.q: What is the equation of a line with slope -2 passing through (0, 5)?
quiz.e: Using slope-intercept form y=mx+b with m=-2 and b=5 (the y-intercept).

quiz.q: If a rectangle has perimeter 30 and length 9, what is the width?
What is the volume of a cylinder with radius 3 and height 10?
o: 9π

quiz.q: Simplify: (2x - 3)(x + 4)
On the ACT, what percentage of the Math section roughly involves geometry, statistics, and probability combined?
quiz.e: Roughly 40% of ACT Math covers geometry, statistics, and probability; the rest is algebra/functions.

quiz.q: What is the mean of {2, 4, 6, 8, 10}?
quiz.e: Sum = 30, divided by 5 values = 6.

quiz.q: Solve: |2x - 4| = 10
o: x=7 or x=-3
x=3 or x=-7
x=7 only
x=-3 only

quiz.q: What is the value of 4! (4 factorial)?
Which of these represents an inverse variation between x and y?
o: y = kx
y = k/x
y = x + k
y = x^2 + k
quiz.e: Inverse variation means y decreases as x increases, modeled by y=k/x.

quiz.q: Two similar triangles have a scale factor of 3. If the area of the small triangle is 5, what is the area of the large triangle?
quiz.e: Area scales with the square of the linear scale factor: 5 × 3² = 45.

quiz.q: What is the correct simplification of sqrt(50)?
o: 5sqrt(2)
25sqrt(2)
10sqrt(5)
2sqrt(25)
quiz.e: sqrt(50)=sqrt(25×2)=5sqrt(2).

quiz.q: If a car travels 240 miles in 4 hours, what is its average speed?
o: 50 mph
60 mph
70 mph
80 mph
quiz.e: Speed = distance/time = 240/4 = 60 mph.

quiz.q: What is the sum of the interior angles of a hexagon?
Which trap most often causes errors on inequality questions?
o: Flipping the inequality sign when multiplying or dividing both sides by a positive
Flipping the inequality sign when adding or subtracting a number on both sides
Forgetting to flip the inequality sign when multiplying/dividing by a negative
Dropping the inequality sign and treating the statement as an equation to solve
quiz.e: Multiplying or dividing both sides of an inequality by a negative number requires flipping the inequality sign—an easy point to lose.

quiz.q: Solve for x: 2^x = 32
What is the distance between points (1, 2) and (4, 6)?
quiz.e: Distance = sqrt((4-1)²+(6-2)²) = sqrt(9+16) = sqrt(25) = 5.

quiz.q: A question gives a table of x and y values and asks for the pattern's rule. What's the best first step?
o: Find the constant difference or ratio between consecutive values to identify linear vs. exponential pattern
Add up all the y-values and divide by the number of rows to find the average rate of change
Compare only the first and last rows to decide whether the pattern is linear or quadratic
Square each x-value and check whether the y-values match the squares listed in the table
quiz.e: Checking whether differences (linear) or ratios (exponential/geometric) are constant reveals the underlying rule quickly.

quiz.q: Simplify: 3x/6
o: 2x
quiz.e: 3x/6 reduces to x/2 by dividing numerator and denominator by 3.

quiz.q: What is the correct answer for combining like terms: 5x + 3 - 2x + 7?
quiz.e: 5x-2x=3x, and 3+7=10, giving 3x+10.

quiz.q: If the ratio of boys to girls in a class is 3:5 and there are 24 students total, how many girls are there?
quiz.e: Total ratio parts = 8; each part = 24/8 = 3; girls = 5×3 = 15.

quiz.q: On the ACT Math test, calculators are:
o: Not allowed at all
Allowed for the entire section
Allowed only for the last 20 questions
Allowed only for geometry questions
quiz.e: Per current ACT policy, calculators are permitted for the entire Math section.

quiz.q: What is 2/5 expressed as a percent?
Which is the correct formula for the area of a trapezoid with parallel sides b1 and b2 and height h?
o: A = b1×b2×h
A = b1×h + b2×h
quiz.e: The trapezoid area formula averages the two parallel sides and multiplies by the height.

quiz.q: What is the correct value of cos(60°)?
o: sqrt(3)/2
sqrt(2)/2
quiz.e: cos(60°) = 1/2, a standard unit-circle value worth memorizing.

quiz.q: What is the best first step when starting an ACT Reading passage?
o: Memorize the names and dates in the passage before looking at any of the questions
Skim the passage quickly for main idea and structure before reading questions closely
Read the first sentence of each paragraph only and then move straight to the questions
Read the passage slowly once and annotate every detail before looking at any question
quiz.e: An efficient first pass builds a mental map of the passage's main idea and structure, making it easier to locate details later.

quiz.q: A 'detail' question requires which kind of support?
o: A directly stated fact from the passage
A reasonable conclusion drawn from tone
A general fact widely known about the topic
A summary of the passage's overall theme
quiz.e: Detail questions are answerable by finding an explicit statement in the text, not inference.

quiz.q: An 'inference' question asks you to:
o: Restate a sentence from the passage nearly word for word, using only its own wording
Make a broad prediction about the topic drawing mainly on your general knowledge
Draw a small logical step beyond what's explicitly stated, based on textual evidence
Identify the author's personal background by examining the style and word choices
quiz.e: Inference questions require a reasonable conclusion supported by, but not directly stated in, the text.

quiz.q: How many passages appear on the ACT Reading test, and in how much time?
o: 3 passages in 30 minutes
4 passages in 35 minutes
5 passages in 40 minutes
4 passages in 45 minutes
quiz.e: ACT Reading has 4 passages (one of which may be paired) with 40 questions total in 35 minutes.

quiz.q: What are 'paired passages' on the ACT?
o: Two long unrelated passages placed in one slot, each with its own questions
A single passage followed by a shorter response, with comparison questions
A longer passage matched with a chart, including data interpretation questions
Two shorter related passages in one slot, including comparison questions
quiz.e: One of the four Reading slots contains two shorter passages on a related topic, with questions comparing them.

quiz.q: Which approach to line-referenced questions is most efficient?
o: Read only the cited line and answer, since extra context will confuse you
Read the entire paragraph that follows the cited line and ignore the rest
Skim the answer choices first and pick the one using words from the line
Read a few sentences before and after the cited line for context
quiz.e: Reading the surrounding context (not just the exact line) usually reveals the intended meaning without rereading everything.

quiz.q: A vocabulary-in-context question asks the meaning of a word as used in the passage. Best strategy?
o: Choose the answer that matches the word's most common meaning outside this passage
Substitute each answer choice into the sentence and see which preserves the meaning
Select the choice that has the closest spelling or sound to the underlined word
Pick the choice that sounds most formal and fits the author's overall level of style
quiz.e: Words often have secondary meanings; substituting each choice tests which fits the passage's actual context.

quiz.q: Is there a penalty for guessing wrong on the ACT Reading test?
o: Yes, a quarter point is deducted
No, there is no penalty for incorrect answers
Yes, but only in the last passage
Only if you guess more than 5 times
quiz.e: The ACT has no wrong-answer penalty, so every question should be answered, even a blind guess.

quiz.q: Which is a common wrong-answer trap on Reading questions?
o: An answer that paraphrases the passage accurately and fits the question
An answer that matches the author's stated position in the cited lines
An answer that sounds sophisticated but isn't supported by the passage
An answer that uses plain wording to repeat a point in the nearby text
quiz.e: Attractive-sounding but unsupported answers are a classic ACT Reading distractor.

quiz.q: What should you do if a question about the main idea seems to have two plausible answers?
o: Choose the one that focuses on the passage's most memorable example and its supporting details
Choose the one with the broadest, most general scope that fits the entire passage, not just one part
Choose the one that uses the most key terms taken from the passage's opening paragraph
Choose the one with the narrowest focus because specific answers are easier to verify
quiz.e: Main idea answers must reflect the passage as a whole, not just a single paragraph or detail.

quiz.q: 'Must be true' answer choices on Reading questions require:
o: Confirming the statement matches the most likely scenario that the passage states
Checking that the statement uses language similar to the passage's main paragraph
Verifying the statement holds under every scenario supported by the passage
Finding any supporting sentence in the passage that could be read in the same way
quiz.e: A 'must be true' claim can be eliminated by finding even one scenario in the text where it doesn't hold.

quiz.q: Approximately how much time should you budget per Reading passage, including its questions?
o: 3-4 minutes
8-9 minutes
15 minutes
20 minutes
quiz.e: With 35 minutes for 4 passages, roughly 8-9 minutes per passage (including reading and answering) is a good pace.

quiz.q: What does a 'function' question ask about a specific sentence or paragraph?
o: Why the author included it / what purpose it serves in the passage
How the author's choice of words in it differs from the other sentences
Which literary device, such as simile or irony, appears in its wording
Whether its claim is supported by evidence given in the preceding lines
quiz.e: Function questions test understanding of a sentence or paragraph's rhetorical purpose within the passage.

quiz.q: Which reading strategy helps most with pacing on natural science and social science passages?
o: Reading every sentence slowly on the first pass and noting each statistic and name so all later questions can be answered from memory
Reading the first and last paragraphs thoroughly and ignoring the middle paragraphs unless a question names them directly
Noting the topic, main idea, and structure of each paragraph, saving deep detail-hunting for when a question requires it
Skimming only the opening sentence of the passage and then answering each question using general knowledge of the topic
quiz.e: A structural first read (without over-focusing on every detail) speeds up later targeted searches.

quiz.q: In a Prose Fiction/Literary Narrative passage, questions often focus on:
o: Experimental design, variables, and controls
Characters' feelings, relationships, and tone
Statistical trends, sources, and arguments
Historical context, dates, and causes
quiz.e: Literary narrative passages emphasize character, tone, and relationships rather than data or research.

quiz.q: When two answer choices seem almost identical except for one qualifying word (e.g., 'always' vs. 'often'), what should you do?
o: Choose the option with the extreme qualifier, because strong wording shows the author's firm position on the idea
Check the passage carefully—extreme qualifiers like 'always' or 'never' are frequently wrong unless directly supported
Treat the two options as equal and decide using the order of the answer choices instead of the passage
Eliminate the softer option, because moderate qualifiers like 'often' or 'sometimes' are rarely supported by the passage
quiz.e: Extreme language must be explicitly supported by the text; softer qualifiers are safer defaults unless proven otherwise.

quiz.q: What's the benefit of previewing the questions (not answer choices) before reading a passage in some strategies?
o: It lets you answer detail questions from the stems alone and avoid reading most of the text
It makes the order of the passages irrelevant because each question names its own passage
It ensures you will remember each answer choice you saw before reading the passage itself
It lets you know what to look for while reading, improving speed for detail questions
quiz.e: Previewing question topics can help direct attention while reading, though the choice of previewing vs. reading straight through is a personal strategy preference.

quiz.q: A 'comparison' question on a paired-passage set typically asks you to:
o: Decide which author's sentences are longer and more complex in their structure
Summarize the main events from one passage and the setting of the other passage
Identify a similarity or difference in the two authors' views or approaches
Judge which author's conclusion is more likely true based on outside knowledge
quiz.e: Paired-passage comparison questions require synthesizing both passages' perspectives or content.

quiz.q: Which of these is the best sign a chosen Reading answer is correct?
o: It matches the overall mood and general impression the passage leaves with you
It repeats the most sophisticated vocabulary found anywhere in the passage
It agrees with what most test-takers would reasonably assume about the topic
It can be directly traced back to specific wording or ideas in the passage
quiz.e: Correct ACT Reading answers are always traceable to specific textual evidence.

quiz.q: If you're running out of time on the Reading section, what's the best move?
o: Fill in a guess for every remaining question, since there's no penalty
Leave the remaining questions blank, since wrong answers lower your score
Spend the leftover time rereading the first passage to check your earlier answers
Guess only on the questions that look easy and leave the harder ones unanswered
quiz.e: Because wrong answers aren't penalized, guessing on unanswered questions can only help your score.

quiz.q: What kind of question is: 'The passage suggests that the narrator's attitude toward her mother is best described as...'?
o: Detail question
Inference/tone question
Vocabulary-in-context question
Structure question
quiz.e: This asks you to infer attitude/tone from indirect textual cues, not a direct statement.

quiz.q: Which technique helps avoid getting bogged down by a difficult word in a Reading passage?
o: Pause to recall the word's dictionary definition, even if it takes a long while
Skip the whole sentence and the rest of that paragraph until all questions are done
Reread the passage from the beginning until the word's meaning becomes clear
Use context clues from surrounding sentences to infer general meaning and keep moving
quiz.e: Context clues let you infer enough meaning to continue without derailing your pace.

quiz.q: What is the ideal order for tackling ACT Reading passages if you find one genre harder?
o: Always work strictly in printed order, since the passages get steadily easier toward the end
Start with the longest passage first, since it carries the most questions and points
Do the hardest passage type first while you are fresh, saving easy ones for the end
Do your strongest/fastest passage types first to bank points, saving harder ones for remaining time
quiz.e: Since all passages count equally, tackling easier passages first secures points before time pressure builds.

quiz.q: A question states, 'Which choice most clearly indicates that the character feels regret?' This requires:
o: Finding a sentence that literally uses the word 'regret' or a direct synonym in the passage
Applying your own experience of how people usually behave when they feel regret
Finding textual evidence (actions, dialogue, description) that supports the inferred emotion
Choosing the most emotionally dramatic option, since regret is a strong feeling
quiz.e: Emotion/inference questions need supporting textual evidence, even if the emotion word itself isn't stated.

quiz.q: Why is rereading the entire passage for every single question an inefficient strategy?
o: It wastes limited time; targeted rereading of relevant sections is faster and just as accurate
It lowers your score, since the ACT penalizes rereading sections you have already covered
It is not permitted, since test rules limit how often you may return to the passage
It causes you to forget the main idea, which hurts accuracy on every later question
quiz.e: With strict time limits, full rereads for each question would use up more time than the section allows.

quiz.q: On paired passages, if a question asks how the author of Passage B would likely respond to a claim in Passage A, you should:
o: Only consider Passage B's content and tone toward that claim
Ignore Passage B and just answer based on Passage A
Use outside knowledge of the topic
Pick the answer that agrees with Passage A regardless of B's view
quiz.e: You must reason about Passage B's specific stance to predict how its author would react to Passage A's claim.

quiz.q: Which is the most efficient way to handle a long, dense sentence during your first read of a passage?
o: Read it slowly several times right away so no detail is missed in the first pass
Underline each key phrase in the sentence before moving on to the next one
Get the gist and move on—come back only if a question specifically requires that sentence's detail
Skip the surrounding paragraph and return to it only after finishing all the questions
quiz.e: Getting the general gist and returning only if needed keeps your pace steady across the whole passage.

quiz.q: A 'least supported' or 'EXCEPT' question asks you to find:
o: The one answer choice most strongly supported by the passage, while the other three are not
The answer choice that most clearly states the passage's main idea or central claim
The one answer choice NOT supported by the passage, while the other three are
The one choice that is only partly supported, while the other three are fully contradicted
quiz.e: EXCEPT/LEAST questions invert the usual logic—three choices are supported and one is not (or vice versa, per the question's wording).

quiz.q: Which best describes how ACT Reading passages are typically ordered by genre across the test (though order can vary by form)?
o: Social Science, Natural Science, Humanities, and Prose Fiction, always in that exact order
Prose Fiction, Poetry, Social Science, and Humanities, with one passage from each category
Natural Science, Social Science, Business, and Humanities, drawn only from nonfiction articles
Prose Fiction/Literary Narrative, Social Science, Humanities, and Natural Science
quiz.e: ACT Reading traditionally draws from four genre categories: Literary Narrative, Social Science, Humanities, and Natural Science.

quiz.q: If a question references 'lines 45-52,' what's the smartest approach?
o: Read only the cited lines 45-52 and nothing around them, since extra text can mislead you
Read lines 45-52 plus a sentence or two before/after for context
Reread the whole passage from the first line so you understand the overall context
Read from line 45 to the end of the passage to see how the section is resolved
quiz.e: Reading slightly beyond the cited lines often reveals context needed to answer correctly without a full reread.

quiz.q: A student consistently runs out of time on the last Reading passage. What's a good fix?
o: Spend extra time on the first passages so the last one feels more manageable
Read the final passage first on test day and then return to the earlier ones
Practice full passages under timed conditions to build pacing awareness and speed
Read each passage more slowly and carefully so that every detail is absorbed
quiz.e: Timed practice builds the pacing instincts needed to allocate roughly equal time across all four passages.

quiz.q: Which statement about correct ACT Reading answers is most accurate?
o: They are usually the choice with the most general, widely agreeable wording about the topic
They often depend on background knowledge of the subject matter beyond the passage
They are typically the choice that makes the strongest, most absolute claim about the author
They are almost always directly supported by specific text, not just plausible-sounding
quiz.e: ACT Reading answers are text-based; the correct choice is provable from what's written, not from general plausibility.

quiz.q: When two passages present conflicting viewpoints on the same topic, what should you track while reading?
o: Which author uses the more persuasive style, so you can pick the stronger of the two
Each author's tone and word choice, so you can decide which view the test favors
Each author's central claim and key supporting reasons, so you can compare them accurately
Only the points where the authors agree, since questions rarely ask about differences
quiz.e: Tracking each author's claim and reasoning is essential for accurately answering comparison questions.

quiz.q: What's the risk of picking an answer just because it 'sounds smart' with big vocabulary?
o: Little risk, since sophisticated wording usually signals the choice the test-makers intended
It guarantees the choice is correct, since the ACT rewards precise academic vocabulary
It matters only on passages that discuss science, where technical terms are common
It may not be supported by the passage at all—a classic ACT distractor pattern
quiz.e: The ACT frequently uses sophisticated-sounding wrong answers to tempt test-takers away from the text-supported choice.

quiz.q: A 'sequence of events' question asks you to:
o: Estimate the date or era in which the passage was written from its style and details
Determine the correct chronological order of events described in the passage
Count how many separate events or scenes the passage describes from start to finish
Decide which event in the passage had the greatest effect on the narrator or author
quiz.e: These questions require tracking the order in which events occur or are revealed in the text.

quiz.q: If you finish a Reading passage's questions early, what's a good use of remaining time?
o: Rest quietly, since extra review rarely changes answers and may only cause doubt
Change several answers you felt sure about, since first instincts are usually wrong
Double check any answers you were unsure about, using text evidence to confirm
Start rereading the other passages in the section to get ahead on later questions
quiz.e: Reviewing uncertain answers with fresh eyes, grounded in text evidence, is a productive use of extra time.

quiz.q: A passage's main idea/theme is usually best captured by considering:
o: The first paragraph alone, since authors state the entire main idea at the beginning
The most vivid or detailed example in the passage, since it reveals the author's point
The title and the opening sentence together, without reading the rest of the passage
The introduction, key transitions, and conclusion together
quiz.e: The overall theme emerges from how the introduction, development, and conclusion work together, not from any single line.

quiz.q: Which is the best definition of 'skimming' as an ACT Reading strategy?
o: Reading every sentence slowly and carefully so you can memorize the passage's details
Reading the questions and answer choices first and never looking at the passage itself
Reading only the first and last sentence of each paragraph and skipping the middle
Quickly moving through the passage to grasp structure and main ideas, without dwelling on every detail
quiz.e: Skimming is a fast initial read for gist and structure, saving detailed rereading for specific questions.

quiz.q: A question asks for the passage's overall tone. Which is the best approach?
o: Judge tone from the topic alone, since subject matter determines how the author feels
Judge tone from word choice, sentence structure, and content across the whole passage
Pick the most extreme emotional option, since ACT authors usually write with strong feeling
Judge tone only from the last paragraph, since it shows the author's final attitude
quiz.e: Tone should be assessed holistically from diction, imagery, and content patterns across the passage, not a single word or title.

quiz.q: Which is true about how ACT Reading questions are ordered within a passage's question set?
o: They follow passage order exactly, so each answer is found just after the previous one
They run from easiest to hardest, so later questions need the most careful rereading
They are grouped by type, so all detail questions come first, then inference questions
They are not necessarily in passage order, so don't assume question 3 comes before question 4 in the text
quiz.e: ACT Reading questions are not guaranteed to follow the passage's line order, so locating evidence for each question independently matters.

quiz.q: How many passages and questions appear on the ACT Science test?
o: 4 passages, 40 questions
6-7 passages, 40 questions
5 passages, 35 questions
6 passages, 60 questions
quiz.e: ACT Science has 6-7 passages totaling 40 questions in 35 minutes.

quiz.q: What percentage of ACT Science questions can typically be answered directly from given data, without outside science knowledge?
quiz.e: About 90% of Science questions are answerable purely from the provided figures, tables, and text.

quiz.q: On a graph, which axis conventionally represents the independent variable?
o: The y-axis (vertical)
The x-axis (horizontal)
Neither, it's random
Both equally
quiz.e: By convention, the independent variable (the one manipulated) is plotted on the x-axis.

quiz.q: What is a 'Data Representation' passage type on ACT Science?
o: A passage that describes a single experiment step by step and explains why each result occurred
A passage that presents two scientists' competing explanations, supported by short written arguments
A passage centered on graphs, tables, or charts with questions about reading and interpreting the data
A passage built around a lab procedure, with questions on safety and equipment choices
quiz.e: Data Representation passages emphasize interpreting given graphs/tables rather than following an experiment.

quiz.q: What defines a 'Research Summaries' passage?
o: It presents two or more scientists' competing explanations that you must compare in writing
It describes one or more experiments (methods and results) that you must analyze
It is built mainly around a single graph, with questions on reading values from the axes
It gives general background on a scientific topic with no experiments or measured results
quiz.e: Research Summaries passages describe experimental design and results across one or more related studies.

quiz.q: What defines a 'Conflicting Viewpoints' passage?
o: Several related experiments whose methods and results you must analyze using tables and graphs
One scientist's hypothesis supported by a detailed graph, with questions on reading trends
Two or more scientists/hypotheses that disagree about the same phenomenon, evaluated via text only (usually no data)
Two scientists who agree on a phenomenon but use different experiments to support the same view
quiz.e: Conflicting Viewpoints passages present differing scientific hypotheses to compare and evaluate.

quiz.q: If a question asks about a trend beyond the range of plotted data, this is called:
o: Interpolation
Extrapolation
Correlation
Regression
quiz.e: Extrapolation is predicting values outside the given data range—riskier and less certain than interpolation.

quiz.q: What is 'interpolation'?
o: Estimating a value between two known data points on a graph or table
Estimating a value beyond the highest or lowest data point by extending the trend line
Calculating the exact average of every value shown in a table or graph
Identifying the single highest value among the known data points in a table
quiz.e: Interpolation estimates within the range of existing data, which is safer than extrapolating beyond it.

quiz.q: A question asks which experimental trial had the highest reaction rate. What's the best approach?
o: Pick the trial that had the largest value for the independent variable being changed
Reread the passage's experimental description and choose the trial it describes last
Scan the relevant table or graph column for the maximum value across trials
Use what you know about reaction kinetics to decide which trial should be fastest
quiz.e: Direct data-reading (finding the max value in the data) answers this without needing outside knowledge.

quiz.q: In Conflicting Viewpoints, if Scientist 1 and Scientist 2 disagree about a planet's formation, a question asking 'with which statement would Scientist 2 most likely agree' requires:
o: Choosing the statement that Scientist 1 would reject, since the two always disagree on everything
Finding the statement that best reflects the evidence both scientists accept in common
Understanding Scientist 2's specific claims and reasoning, then matching them to the choice
Picking the statement that is most scientifically accurate based on what you learned in class
quiz.e: You must trace the logic specific to Scientist 2's stated hypothesis to predict agreement.

quiz.q: Which is the most efficient first step when starting a Science passage?
o: Read every paragraph of the passage in full, then look at the figures only if a question asks
Glance at the figures/tables and passage type first, noting variables and units, before diving into questions
Jump straight to the first question and search the passage only for words that appear in it
Memorize the numbers in each table so you can answer without going back to the figures
quiz.e: Scanning figures and identifying variables/units up front builds a framework for answering data questions quickly.

quiz.q: A question shows two scientists with opposing views on climate change causes. What type of passage is this most likely?
o: Data Representation
Research Summaries
Conflicting Viewpoints
None of the ACT Science passage types
quiz.e: Opposing viewpoints/hypotheses on the same phenomenon define the Conflicting Viewpoints passage type.

quiz.q: If a table shows temperature increasing steadily as pressure increases, which relationship is shown?
o: Positive correlation
Negative correlation
No correlation
Inverse relationship only for gases
quiz.e: Both variables increasing together indicates a positive correlation.

quiz.q: What should you check first when comparing data across multiple similar graphs in a Research Summaries passage?
o: That the graph titles are worded similarly, since similar titles mean the scales match
That the axes/units are the same in each graph before directly comparing values
That the data points on each graph form the same overall trend before comparing values
That each graph has the same number of data points, so the comparison is fair
quiz.e: Different graphs can use different scales or units, so verifying this avoids comparison errors.

quiz.q: On the ACT Science test, why should you avoid relying heavily on outside content knowledge?
o: Because outside knowledge is always wrong
Because most questions are answerable, and expected to be answered, using only the given data—outside assumptions can lead you astray from what the passage says
Because science isn't tested on the ACT
Because using it takes exactly one hour
quiz.e: The Science test primarily assesses data interpretation and reasoning skills, not memorized content, so passage-given information should drive your answer.

quiz.q: Which pacing approach works best for Science, given its density?
o: Budget about 10 minutes for the first passages and rush through the final ones at the end
Spend as long as needed on each passage until you fully understand it before answering
Budget roughly 5 minutes per passage, moving on if stuck rather than getting bogged down
Read the passage text in full first, then use whatever time remains to answer the questions
quiz.e: With 35 minutes across 6-7 passages, roughly 5 minutes per passage keeps pace steady across the section.

quiz.q: What is the dependent variable in an experiment testing how fertilizer amount affects plant height?
o: Fertilizer amount
Plant height
Sunlight exposure
Soil type
quiz.e: Plant height is measured as a result of the manipulated variable (fertilizer amount), making it the dependent variable.

quiz.q: A question asks for the value of y when x=15, but the table only shows x=10 and x=20. What must you do?
o: Interpolate between the two known values
Extrapolate beyond the data
State it cannot be determined
Only use the x=10 value
quiz.e: Since 15 lies between the two known values (10 and 20), interpolation is appropriate.

quiz.q: What is a control group in an experiment?
o: A group receiving a larger dose of the tested variable, used to magnify its effect
A group whose measurements are averaged over many trials, used to reduce random error
The group that the experimenters expect to show the strongest result in the experiment
A baseline group not receiving the variable being tested, used for comparison
quiz.e: A control group provides a baseline without the tested variable, letting you isolate its effect.

quiz.q: If a question says a hypothesis is 'supported' by data, what must be true?
o: The data trend matches what the hypothesis predicted
The data contradicts the hypothesis
There is no data at all
The hypothesis is definitely proven for all cases
quiz.e: 'Supported' means the observed data is consistent with the hypothesis's prediction, not proof beyond all doubt.

quiz.q: Which is a common ACT Science trap regarding two similar-looking answer choices?
o: One choice repeats the data accurately, while the other states the same trend using different wording
One choice reverses the actual trend shown (e.g., swaps increasing for decreasing)
One choice uses a unit that was never mentioned anywhere in the passage's figures
One choice is always correct, so the other can be eliminated without checking the data
quiz.e: A frequent trap is a choice that inverts or slightly misstates the real data trend.

quiz.q: In a multi-experiment passage, if Experiment 2 changes one variable that Experiment 1 held constant, a question is likely testing:
o: Your ability to recall the procedure of Experiment 1 without referring back to the passage
Your knowledge of which experiment is more reliable based on how many trials it used
Your ability to predict outcomes using outside formulas rather than the experiments' data
Your ability to compare how that specific variable affected results between experiments
quiz.e: Comparing corresponding results across experiments that differ by one variable tests understanding of that variable's specific effect.

quiz.q: When reading a scatter plot in ACT Science, what indicates a strong positive correlation?
o: Points scatter widely above and below a flat horizontal line with no clear direction
Points cluster tightly along a downward-sloping trend line from left to right
Points cluster tightly along an upward-sloping trend line
Points are spread evenly across the whole graph with a few extreme outliers
quiz.e: Tightly clustered points following an upward trend indicate variables increasing together (positive correlation).

quiz.q: A question provides a graph with only 3 data points and asks you to predict the value far past the last point. This is risky because:
o: The graph has too few points to show any trend at all, so any prediction is impossible
The trend line would have to be curved, which makes prediction with three points inaccurate
The ACT treats any prediction beyond the data as a wrong answer regardless of the trend
Extrapolation assumes the trend continues unchanged, which may not hold true outside the observed range
quiz.e: With limited data, extrapolating far beyond it carries more uncertainty since the underlying trend might not continue.

quiz.q: How should you approach a question requiring you to combine information from two different figures in the same passage?
o: Identify the specific quantity needed from each figure and connect them using their shared variable/units
Pick the figure with more data points and apply its values to both parts of the question
Average the highest values from each figure, since the two should agree closely
Use the passage's text to estimate both values, then check them only if time remains
quiz.e: Combining data means pulling the relevant value from each figure and linking them through a common variable.

quiz.q: Which best describes how ACT Science 'Conflicting Viewpoints' passages usually present data?
o: Primarily text-based descriptions of each hypothesis, with minimal or no data figures
Large tables of measured results for each hypothesis, with graphs comparing their predictions
Several experiments with detailed methods and results that support each scientist's position
A single graph that both scientists use to support opposite explanations of the phenomenon
quiz.e: Conflicting Viewpoints relies mainly on textual reasoning rather than data figures, unlike Data Representation or Research Summaries.

quiz.q: If a passage defines a term (e.g., 'solubility') specifically for that experiment, what should guide your answers?
o: Your own class definition, since textbook meanings are the standard the ACT expects
The passage's given definition, even if it differs slightly from a standard definition
The most common dictionary meaning, since it applies in any scientific setting
A blend of the passage's wording and your own knowledge, whichever seems more complete
quiz.e: ACT Science expects you to use the passage's own operational definitions, since science questions are self-contained.

quiz.q: A bar graph shows reaction rates for 4 different catalysts. A question asks which catalyst is least effective. Best approach?
o: Read the bar with the lowest reaction rate value directly from the graph
Choose the catalyst with the tallest bar, since a higher rate means less effectiveness
Choose the catalyst whose name sounds least familiar from your chemistry classes
Choose the bar closest to the average of all four, since it is the typical performer
quiz.e: This is a direct data-reading question solvable by comparing bar heights/values.

quiz.q: What is the best way to handle unfamiliar scientific vocabulary in a Science passage?
o: Pause and sound out the word's prefixes and suffixes until you can recall its meaning from class
Skip every question that includes the term, since it can't be answered without it
Use the passage's context and any given definitions/units to understand its role in the data
Search the passage for a similar-looking word and assume the two mean the same thing
quiz.e: Passages are self-contained; you don't need outside vocabulary knowledge if you use the passage's own context and data.

quiz.q: In Research Summaries, if Experiment 1 and Experiment 2 use the same setup but different temperatures, a comparison question tests:
o: How well you remember general facts about temperature from earlier science courses
The isolated effect of temperature on the measured outcome
Which of the two experiments had more trials or more data points in its table
How the change in the setup itself, rather than temperature, shifted the outcome
quiz.e: When only one variable differs between otherwise identical experiments, its effect is what any comparison question targets.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT typically tested on ACT Science?
o: Reading values from a table or graph to answer questions about specific trials
Predicting how an outcome changes using trends shown in the passage's data
Judging which of two hypotheses is better supported by the evidence presented
Recalling advanced memorized scientific formulas from outside the passage
quiz.e: ACT Science tests reasoning and data interpretation skills based on the passage, not memorized outside formulas.

quiz.q: A question asks you to identify a flaw in an experiment's design. Which is a common flaw to look for?
o: Using a large enough sample of trials to make the experiment's results reliable
Failure to control for a variable that could affect the outcome, confounding the results
Changing only one variable at a time while all other conditions stay the same
Including a control group to compare against the group receiving the treatment
quiz.e: Uncontrolled variables can confound results, making this a classic experimental design flaw the ACT tests.

quiz.q: How should conflicting data points ('outliers') on a graph be treated when identifying an overall trend?
o: Ignore the overall trend and use the outlier as the answer
Recognize them as departures from the general pattern but still describe the overall trend accurately when asked
Delete them from consideration entirely without noting them
Assume the graph is wrong
quiz.e: Outliers should be recognized as such, but general trend questions still require describing the pattern of the majority of data.

quiz.q: If two passages' data support opposite conclusions about the same variable, and a question asks you to reconcile them, what matters most?
o: Choosing the passage with the larger data set, since more data always outweighs fewer data
Splitting the difference between the two conclusions and choosing the answer in the middle
Carefully comparing each passage's specific experimental conditions/data supporting its own conclusion
Relying on the passage's authors' reputations rather than on how their data were gathered
quiz.e: Reconciling requires analyzing how each passage's specific setup and data lead to its distinct conclusion.

quiz.q: A figure shows pH decreasing as a chemical is added. A question asks what happens to pH if twice as much chemical is added, within the tested range. Best approach?
o: Predict that pH will rise slightly, since doubling the chemical must reverse the trend
State that pH cannot be estimated, since the exact amount tested was not listed
Apply a pH formula from chemistry class and ignore the pattern in the figure
Interpolate/extend the observed trend within the data's range to estimate the new pH
quiz.e: If the amount stays within or near the tested range, you can reason from the observed trend in the data.

quiz.q: Which is the correct order of a typical Research Summaries passage's content?
o: A short list of data tables followed by a conclusion with no description of methods
Two scientists' opposing hypotheses, followed by evidence supporting each position
Detailed results first, then the background, with no explanation of how it was tested
Introduction/background, description of experimental setup(s), and results (tables/graphs)
quiz.e: Research Summaries passages walk through background, methodology, and results in that general structure.

quiz.q: Two graphs use different y-axis scales (one 0-10, one 0-1000). What's the risk of comparing them without noticing?
o: Values may look equally large on both graphs, hiding a difference of a hundredfold in size
The graphs may seem to show opposite trends when the data actually move together
Misreading relative magnitude, thinking values are more/less similar than they actually are
Both graphs will have different titles, which makes the comparison impossible to check
quiz.e: Ignoring differing scales can lead to badly wrong conclusions about how the data sets relate.

quiz.q: When a question asks 'based on the passage, which statement is a hypothesis rather than an observation,' you should look for:
o: A measured result recorded in a table, such as the temperature at which a sample melted
A predictive claim proposed to explain a phenomenon, not yet directly measured
A statement of fact the scientist observed directly in the lab during the experiment
A claim that has already been confirmed by repeated trials and is now accepted as true
quiz.e: A hypothesis is a proposed explanation/prediction, distinct from directly observed/measured data.

quiz.q: If Scientist 1 believes a crater was formed by a meteor impact and Scientist 2 believes it was formed by volcanic activity, a question asking for evidence that would weaken Scientist 1's view requires:
o: Evidence inconsistent with a meteor impact but potentially consistent with volcanic origin
Evidence supporting both a meteor impact and a volcanic origin about equally well
Evidence that a meteor impact produced the crater, which supports Scientist 1's view
Evidence that disproves volcanic activity, which would indirectly strengthen the impact view
quiz.e: Weakening a viewpoint means finding evidence that contradicts its specific claims.

quiz.q: What's the fastest way to answer a question asking to identify a specific numeric value from a table with many rows and columns?
o: Locate the correct row and column intersection matching the question's specified conditions directly
Scan every row of the whole table and average the numbers that look closest to it
Read the passage's description of the experiment and estimate the value from the text
Find the largest value in the relevant column and choose it as the closest answer
quiz.e: Precisely locating the row/column intersection specified by the question is the direct, fast route to the answer.

quiz.q: Is the ACT Writing test included in the Composite score?
o: Yes, always
No, it is optional and reported separately
Only if you score above a 30
Only for certain states
quiz.e: The Writing test is optional and does not factor into the 1-36 Composite score.

quiz.q: How long is the ACT Writing test?
o: 20 minutes
30 minutes
40 minutes
60 minutes
quiz.e: Test-takers are given 40 minutes to plan and write the essay.

quiz.q: On what scale is the ACT essay scored?
quiz.e: The essay receives a score from 2-12, the sum of four domain scores each averaged from two graders' 1-6 ratings.

quiz.q: How many domains make up the ACT Writing score?
o: Two
Three
Four
Five
quiz.e: The four domains are Ideas & Analysis, Development & Support, Organization, and Language Use.

quiz.q: The ACT essay prompt presents how many given perspectives on an issue?
o: One
Two
Three
Four
quiz.e: The prompt provides three different perspectives on a debatable issue for the student to engage with.

quiz.q: What is required regarding the given perspectives in a high-scoring ACT essay?
o: Agree with all three perspectives equally and summarize each one without evaluating any
Argue against the perspectives without referring to their assumptions or implications
Engage with at least one of the three perspectives, analyzing its assumptions or implications
Focus on one perspective and quote it at length without adding any analysis of your own
quiz.e: Strong essays analyze at least one given perspective, showing critical engagement rather than ignoring the prompt's framework.

quiz.q: Which best describes the 'Ideas & Analysis' domain?
o: The quality and depth of your critical thinking about the issue and perspectives
How accurately you use grammar, punctuation, and sentence structure throughout the essay
How clearly the essay is organized into an introduction, body paragraphs, and conclusion
How many specific examples and details you include to support each claim you make
quiz.e: This domain assesses how thoughtfully you generate and analyze ideas about the issue.

quiz.q: Which best describes the 'Development & Support' domain?
o: How well you explain and support your ideas with reasoning, examples, or evidence
How logically the essay moves from the introduction through its paragraphs to a conclusion
How original and insightful your thinking about the issue and its perspectives appears
How varied your sentences are and how precise your word choice is throughout the essay
quiz.e: This domain rewards well-explained, well-supported reasoning rather than vague, unsupported assertions.

quiz.q: Which best describes the 'Organization' domain?
o: The logical structure and flow of the essay, including transitions and paragraphing
How strong your ideas about the issue are and how deeply you analyze each perspective
How many examples and details you include to back up each of your main claims
How accurate your grammar and word choice are across the whole of the essay
quiz.e: Organization assesses whether ideas are arranged logically with clear transitions between them.

quiz.q: Which best describes the 'Language Use' domain?
o: The depth of your critical thinking about the issue and the perspectives it presents
The logical order of your paragraphs and the transitions that connect them to each other
How well you support your claims with specific reasoning, examples, and evidence
Command of grammar, word choice, sentence variety, and clarity of expression
quiz.e: Language Use evaluates the mechanics and stylistic control of your writing, similar to composition skills tested in English.

quiz.q: Does essay length alone guarantee a higher score?
o: Yes, longer essays always score higher because they show more development and detail
Yes, as long as the essay is at least four full pages with neat paragraphs
No, a well-organized and well-supported shorter essay can outscore a long, unfocused one
No, because the graders look only at your thesis and ignore the rest of the essay
quiz.e: Quality of reasoning, support, and organization matters more than raw length.

quiz.q: Why might a student choose to take the ACT Writing test even though it's optional?
o: Colleges that require it use the writing score to replace your English score in admissions
Taking it raises the Composite score because it adds points to the 1-36 scale
Some colleges request or recommend writing scores as part of admissions
It is required for students who score below a certain level on the English test
quiz.e: Certain colleges ask for the Writing score, so students should check target schools' requirements.

quiz.q: What is a common weakness in essays that only restate the three given perspectives?
o: They repeat each perspective accurately, which earns top marks for Language Use alone
They spend too much time on grammar, which lowers the Organization domain score
They fail to develop the writer's own distinct argument, hurting Ideas & Analysis and Development scores
They run out of time before the conclusion, which automatically lowers every domain score
quiz.e: Merely summarizing given perspectives without building your own argument limits depth of analysis.

quiz.q: What is a strong way to open an ACT essay?
o: A broad quotation about the topic that never mentions your actual position on the issue
A clear statement of your position/thesis relevant to the specific issue given
A long summary of each of the three perspectives before you say anything of your own
A question to the reader about the issue, followed by several background facts and no thesis
quiz.e: A clear, relevant thesis early on helps graders quickly see your position and sets up the analysis to follow.

quiz.q: Which is true about time management on the Writing test?
o: A few minutes of planning/outlining before writing usually improves organization and coherence
Planning can wait until the conclusion, when you know what the essay actually argues
Using the full 40 minutes to write yields the most developed essay with the best flow
Planning matters only for essays you expect to be long, and it can be skipped for short ones
quiz.e: Brief planning time helps structure the essay's argument and improves the Organization domain score.

quiz.q: What does 'analyzing the relationships between perspectives' mean on the ACT essay?
o: Summarizing each perspective in turn and noting which one is the most common viewpoint
Choosing the perspective you like best and using it as the central thesis of your essay
Listing the differences in vocabulary among the perspectives and the writers' tones
Discussing how perspectives agree, disagree, or share underlying assumptions, not just describing each one separately
quiz.e: Top-scoring essays often explore how the given perspectives relate to each other, not just describe each in isolation.

quiz.q: Which type of evidence strengthens the Development & Support domain most?
o: General statements about the topic that most readers would readily agree are true
Quotations from famous authors that are only loosely related to the essay's main claim
A long list of facts and statistics presented without any reasoning about their meaning
Specific, relevant examples or reasoning that clearly support your claims
quiz.e: Concrete, relevant support (examples, reasoning) demonstrates depth in the Development & Support domain.

quiz.q: How are the two 1-6 domain scores combined into the final 2-12 domain score for each of the four domains?
o: Multiplied together
Averaged together, then this average is used across all four domains to reach 2-12 range per domain, and overall a composite writing score is formed
Only the higher score counts
Only the lower score counts
quiz.e: Two graders independently score each domain 1-6; those two scores combine per domain (typically summed to a 2-12 domain score).

quiz.q: If a student runs out of time and doesn't finish the conclusion, what's the primary risk?
