o: A score of zero in every domain, since an essay without a conclusion cannot be graded
Weaker Organization and possibly Development scores from an incomplete argument
A lower Language Use score only, since the unfinished part contains grammar mistakes
Its Ideas & Analysis score is lowered, though the other three domains are unaffected
quiz.e: An abrupt, unfinished ending can hurt how organized and complete the argument appears to graders.

quiz.q: Which is a better essay conclusion strategy?
o: Restate every point from your essay one by one, in the same order and in the same words
Close with a new argument that expands your position beyond what the body paragraphs covered
Briefly synthesize your argument and its significance, tying back to the thesis
End with a quotation from another source and leave the thesis unmentioned
quiz.e: A strong conclusion reinforces the thesis and shows the argument's significance without introducing unrelated new points.

quiz.q: What role does sentence variety play in the ACT essay score?
o: It is scored under Organization, since varied sentences help paragraphs flow together
It matters only for essays over a certain length, where repetition would be noticeable
It is judged under Development & Support, since longer sentences hold more evidence
It's assessed under Language Use, showing writing skill and reducing monotony
quiz.e: Varied sentence structure demonstrates stronger command of language, which the Language Use domain rewards.

quiz.q: Which statement about grammar errors on the ACT essay is most accurate?
o: Even minor errors lower your score evenly, whether or not they affect the reader's understanding
Grammar is scored only when an essay is otherwise well organized and well supported
Occasional minor errors are less damaging than errors that interfere with clarity or meaning
Errors matter only when they appear in the introduction, where graders form their first impression
quiz.e: Language Use considers how errors affect clarity/meaning, not just their raw presence, though excessive errors do hurt scores.

quiz.q: A student wants to address a potential counterargument to their thesis. Where is this best placed?
o: In the conclusion alone, so that the introduction and body stay focused on your own view
Within the body, where it can be acknowledged and responded to, strengthening the overall analysis
In the introduction only, before you state your thesis and begin the main argument
In a separate note at the end of the essay, after the conclusion has been written
quiz.e: Addressing counterarguments in the body strengthens the essay's depth of analysis and shows nuanced thinking.

quiz.q: Which best summarizes what makes a top-scoring ACT essay different from an average one?
o: It uses a confident tone and a wide range of vocabulary, whatever the actual quality of its analysis
It shows nuanced, well-organized analysis of the issue and perspectives, backed by specific support, in clear language
It restates each perspective accurately and in the same order as the prompt presents them
It covers as many different points as possible in the time allowed, with brief support for each
quiz.e: Top essays combine depth of analysis, strong organization, solid support, and controlled language—not just length or vocabulary.

quiz.q: What kind of topic does the ACT Writing prompt typically present?
o: A narrow, technical question that has a single correct answer and needs specialized knowledge
A personal reflection about your own experiences, with no connection to other viewpoints
A fictional scenario in which you describe how a character would respond to a problem
A broad, debatable issue relevant to students' lives, with multiple reasonable viewpoints
quiz.e: The prompt centers on a debatable issue where reasonable people can disagree, prompting analysis of multiple perspectives.

quiz.q: Which is a weaker way to use the three given perspectives?
o: Analyzing the assumptions underlying one perspective
Simply listing all three without any analysis or personal argument
Explaining why you agree or disagree with a perspective, with reasoning
Comparing two perspectives and noting where they conflict
quiz.e: Listing perspectives without analysis fails to demonstrate the critical thinking the Ideas & Analysis domain rewards.

quiz.q: A student's essay presents a clear thesis but never explains why their reasoning supports it. Which domain suffers most?
o: Development & Support
Language Use only
None, this doesn't affect scoring
Ideas & Analysis is unaffected
quiz.e: Without explained reasoning behind claims, the Development & Support domain score will be low.

quiz.q: Which best describes a well-organized essay structure for the ACT essay?
o: Several short paragraphs that each restate the thesis in different words without adding points
A single long body paragraph that covers every idea, followed by a short closing sentence
An opening paragraph followed by a list of facts, with no concluding paragraph to tie them up
Introduction with thesis, body paragraphs each developing a distinct point, and a conclusion
quiz.e: A clear introduction-body-conclusion structure with distinct developed points supports strong Organization scores.

quiz.q: Why is it risky to write about a completely unrelated personal topic instead of addressing the prompt's issue?
o: It shows creativity, which graders reward in the Ideas & Analysis domain above all else
It is acceptable as long as the essay is well organized and has clear sentences
It lowers only the Language Use score, because the grammar is judged against the topic
It fails to engage with the assigned issue and perspectives, hurting Ideas & Analysis and relevance
quiz.e: Essays must respond to the specific issue and perspectives given; going off-topic undermines the core requirements.

quiz.q: What is the benefit of using specific, concrete examples rather than vague generalities in the essay?
o: They make the essay longer, which is the main thing the Development & Support domain rewards
Specific examples make your reasoning more persuasive and demonstrate the Development & Support domain effectively
They help only with Language Use, since concrete words are more precise than abstract ones
They matter little, since graders mainly judge a thesis and the quality of the conclusion
quiz.e: Concrete detail strengthens the persuasiveness and depth of your supporting reasoning.

quiz.q: How should transitions be used between paragraphs in the ACT essay?
o: Placed only at the start of the essay, so the reader knows the order of the points to come
Used in every sentence, so that the reader is always told how each idea connects
Used to clearly connect ideas and show logical relationships between paragraphs
Replaced with short headings at the start of each paragraph, as in a report
quiz.e: Effective transitions clarify how ideas connect, which supports strong Organization scoring.

quiz.q: If two graders give different domain scores for the same essay, what typically happens?
o: The higher of the two scores is used, since graders are assumed to be right when they disagree
A third grader scores the essay again, and that score alone replaces both of the first two
Their scores for that domain are combined (e.g., averaged/summed) per ACT's scoring procedure
The essay is sent to the writer's school, which decides which of the scores to count
quiz.e: ACT Writing uses two independent graders per domain, and their scores are combined per the scoring procedure.

quiz.q: Which is a stronger essay strategy regarding the writer's own perspective?
o: Adopt a view that avoids all of the given perspectives, so your essay stands out as original
Develop your own perspective, which may build on, differ from, or synthesize the given ones, with clear reasoning
State your own view in the introduction only, then use the body to summarize the three
Choose whichever given perspective has the most support and rephrase it in your own words
quiz.e: A high-scoring essay typically develops the writer's own perspective in relation to the given ones, supported by reasoning.

quiz.q: Which of these essay openings best sets up a strong argument?
o: A question with no clear answer, leaving your position ambiguous throughout
A concise thesis that clearly states your position on the issue
A long unrelated anecdote with no connection to the thesis
Repeating the prompt's exact wording with no added insight
quiz.e: Clarity of thesis from the start helps the reader (and grader) follow your argument's direction.

quiz.q: What is a practical time-management split within the 40-minute Writing test?
o: Spend 20 minutes planning, 15 minutes writing, and 5 minutes reviewing at the end
Write for the full 40 minutes, then use the last minute to add a conclusion
A few minutes planning, most of the time writing, and a couple minutes reviewing at the end
Plan for 5 minutes, write the introduction and conclusion first, and fill in the body afterward
quiz.e: Allocating a short planning phase and brief final review, while spending most time writing, is a practical approach.

quiz.q: Why might discussing the strengths AND weaknesses of a given perspective improve an essay's score?
o: It makes the essay longer, and length is the main factor that graders reward in scoring
It shows the grader that you can summarize each perspective without taking any position
It earns extra points in Language Use because balanced sentences sound more sophisticated
It shows nuanced critical analysis rather than a one-sided oversimplification
quiz.e: Nuanced analysis, including acknowledging valid points and limitations, demonstrates depth valued in Ideas & Analysis.

quiz.q: Which is true regarding essay handwriting/legibility during the paper-based ACT Writing test?
o: Illegible handwriting has no effect on scoring
Graders need to be able to read your essay to score it, so legibility matters practically even though it isn't a named domain
Handwriting is the only thing scored
Typed essays are required in all cases
quiz.e: While not a formal domain, illegible handwriting can prevent graders from properly assessing the essay's actual content.

quiz.q: A student spends the entire 40 minutes writing without ever pausing to organize ideas first. What's a likely consequence?
o: A well-developed argument, because writing continuously leaves more time for each idea
A stronger Language Use score only, since writing without stopping improves fluency
A lower Ideas & Analysis score only, while organization is not affected by the lack of planning
A less coherent structure, since no planning occurred before writing began
quiz.e: Skipping planning often leads to a less logically structured essay, which affects the Organization domain.

quiz.q: When engaging with a given perspective you disagree with, what's the best approach?
o: Summarize it briefly and then spend the rest of the essay arguing against it
Fairly represent it, then explain your reasoning for disagreeing
Agree with part of it for the sake of fairness, even if you do not actually believe it
Describe it in your own words and leave your reason for disagreeing unstated
quiz.e: Fair representation followed by reasoned disagreement demonstrates strong analytical engagement.

quiz.q: Which best reflects how the ACT Writing test relates to the English test's skills?
o: They test the same skills in the same way, so a high English score guarantees a high essay score
Writing tests only your ability to write long, well-formed sentences, which English never does
English tests mechanics and Writing tests only ideas, so no language skills overlap
Both draw on similar language, grammar, and organizational skills, though Writing also requires original argument development
quiz.e: Language Use and Organization domains overlap with skills tested in ACT English, while Writing additionally requires original essay composition.

flashcards.d: The ACT English section gives 45 minutes for 75 questions, about 36 seconds per question, spread across five passages.
The ACT Math section gives 60 minutes for 60 questions, roughly one minute per question, with difficulty generally increasing.
The ACT Reading section gives 35 minutes for 40 questions across four passages, about 8-9 minutes per passage including reading and answering.
The ACT Science section gives 35 minutes for 40 questions across six or seven passages, roughly 5 minutes per passage.
The optional ACT Writing test gives 40 minutes to plan, write, and revise a single essay.
On timed sections, answer every question you find easy on a first pass, then return to skipped or difficult questions on a second pass.
The ACT does not subtract points for wrong answers, so never leave a bubble blank — always fill in a guess before time runs out.
Check the clock at fixed checkpoints (like the halfway point) during each section to confirm you're on pace to finish.
Reserve the last 1-2 minutes of a section to transfer and verify answers on the bubble sheet, avoiding rushed misbubbling at the end.
On Reading and Science, you may answer passages in any order, so tackle the easiest passage first to bank points before harder ones.
On ACT English, recognize when the underlined portion is already correct and concise — NO CHANGE is correct roughly a quarter of the time.
When English answer choices differ mainly in length, the shortest option that remains grammatically correct and complete is usually right.
For 'EXCEPT' or 'LEAST' questions, every wrong answer choice actually fits the criteria — find the one choice that does not.
For vocabulary-in-context questions, plug each answer choice back into the sentence and judge by the passage's context, not the word's most common dictionary meaning.
Science 'Data Representation' questions can usually be answered by directly reading a graph or table, without outside science knowledge.
Only choose 'cannot be determined' on Math questions when the given information is genuinely insufficient — it's often a trap for questions that are solvable.
'Must be true' Reading questions require a statement to hold under every scenario the passage supports; one exception is enough to eliminate it.
Paired-passage questions typically ask how the two authors' viewpoints agree or disagree — locate each author's stance before comparing.
'Writer's goal' questions are graded strictly against the stated purpose in the question, not general writing quality.
When two answer choices differ by one qualifying word (like 'always' vs. 'often'), extreme qualifiers are frequently wrong unless directly supported by the text.
Take complete practice tests under real timing and conditions to build stamina and get an accurate score estimate.
Track every missed question by section and category (e.g., comma usage, inference) to reveal recurring weak spots to target.
Review missed questions within a day of taking a practice test, while your reasoning process is still fresh enough to diagnose mistakes.
Practice with the same wake time, breaks, and no-phone rule as real test day so the actual exam feels familiar.
The ACT is always given in the order English, Math, Reading, Science, then the optional Writing test — practice in that same order.
Calculate the section score improvements needed to reach your composite goal, then prioritize practice on the sections with the most room to grow.
Schedule full practice tests roughly every 1-2 weeks rather than back-to-back, leaving time to review and apply lessons before the next one.
After each practice test, identify which section you ran out of time on and adjust your pacing plan for that section specifically.
Practice with official, retired ACT tests whenever possible — they most accurately reflect real question style and difficulty.
In the week before the real test, reduce full practice tests and shift to light review and confidence-building instead of heavy new drilling.
Two independent clauses incorrectly joined by only a comma; fix with a period, semicolon, or comma+conjunction.
A clause essential to the sentence's meaning (e.g., 'that' clauses); takes no surrounding commas.
A clause with extra, non-essential info (often starting with 'which' or a name+appositive); set off by commas on both sides.
Must follow a complete independent clause; introduces a list, explanation, or quotation—never follows a verb or preposition directly.
Joins two independent clauses without a conjunction, or separates items in a complex list.
An introductory phrase whose implied subject doesn't match the sentence's actual subject, creating illogical meaning.
Items in a list or comparison must share the same grammatical form (all gerunds, all infinitives, etc.).
Repeating the same idea with different words (e.g., 'return back'); the ACT rewards the more concise, non-repetitive choice.
Asks whether a proposed addition/edit accomplishes a specific stated purpose—judge strictly against that stated goal, not general quality.
The answer choice indicating the original underlined text is already correct; correct roughly 25% of the time.
Plugging answer choices into the original equation (starting with a middle value) instead of solving algebraically from scratch.
Substituting a smart specific number for a variable in 'for all x' problems to quickly test which answer choice matches.
a² + b² = c², where c is the hypotenuse of a right triangle; used constantly in ACT geometry.
(y2 - y1)/(x2 - x1); measures the steepness/direction of a line between two points.
a² - b² factors as (a - b)(a + b); a common ACT factoring pattern.
If linear dimensions scale by factor k, area scales by k²and volume scales by k³.
A relationship y = k/x, where y decreases as x increases (contrast with direct variation y = kx).
Mnemonic for right-triangle trig: sin=opposite/hypotenuse, cos=adjacent/hypotenuse, tan=opposite/adjacent.
For a polygon with n sides, the sum of interior angles is (n-2) × 180°.
Multiplying or dividing both sides of an inequality by a negative number reverses the inequality's direction.
Asks for a fact directly and explicitly stated in the passage—no inference required.
Requires a small, text-supported logical step beyond what is explicitly stated.
One ACT Reading slot containing two shorter, related passages with added comparison questions.
A question testing a word's meaning as used in the passage, often a secondary/less common definition.
Asks why the author included a specific sentence or paragraph—its rhetorical purpose in the passage.
Asks you to find the one choice NOT supported by the text, while the others are supported.
Read a sentence or two before and after the cited line, not just the exact line, for full context.
Answer choices with words like 'always' or 'never' are usually wrong unless explicitly proven by the text.
The defining trait of a correct ACT Reading answer: it can be traced back to specific passage wording, not just general plausibility.
An ACT Science passage centered on interpreting given graphs, tables, or charts.
An ACT Science passage describing one or more experiments (methods and results) for analysis.
An ACT Science passage presenting two or more disagreeing hypotheses, evaluated mainly through text.
The variable a scientist deliberately manipulates in an experiment; typically plotted on the x-axis.
The variable measured as an outcome/result of the experiment; typically plotted on the y-axis.
Estimating a value that falls between two known, plotted data points.
Estimating a value beyond the range of the given data—riskier since the trend may not continue.
A baseline group in an experiment that does not receive the tested variable, used for comparison.
An uncontrolled variable that could affect the outcome, making it hard to isolate the true cause.
Positive: both variables increase together. Negative: one increases as the other decreases.
An optional 40-minute essay section not included in the Composite score, but sometimes requested by colleges.
2-12, formed from four domain scores, each an average of two graders' 1-6 ratings.
Ideas & Analysis, Development & Support, Organization, and Language Use.
Three differing viewpoints on an issue provided in the prompt; strong essays engage critically with at least one.
The domain assessing depth and critical thinking in how you engage with the issue and perspectives.
The domain assessing how well claims are explained and backed with reasoning or examples.
The domain assessing logical structure, paragraphing, and transitions in the essay.
The domain assessing grammar, word choice, sentence variety, and clarity of expression.
A clear statement of your position on the issue, ideally established early to guide the essay's structure.
Acknowledging and responding to an opposing view within the body paragraphs, which strengthens analytical depth.

PART_A.q: Which punctuation correctly joins two independent clauses without a conjunction?
o: A comma
A semicolon
An apostrophe
A hyphen
PART_A.e: A semicolon can join two independent clauses on its own; a comma alone creates a comma splice.

PART_A.q: In the sentence "My sister, who lives in Ohio, called me last night," the phrase "who lives in Ohio" is set off by commas because it is:
o: Essential to identifying which sister
Nonessential (extra) information
A comma splice
An introductory phrase
PART_A.e: Nonessential clauses that could be removed without changing the sentence's core meaning are set off by commas on both sides.

PART_A.q: Which revision best fixes the redundancy in "He returned back to the store again"?
o: He returned back to the store again.
He returned to the store.
He returned back, again, to the store.
He returned to the store, again and again.
PART_A.e: "Returned back" and "again" repeat the same idea; ACT concision questions favor the shortest version that keeps the meaning.

PART_A.q: Choose the correct verb: "The list of items on the shelf ___ long."
o: are
is
were
have been
PART_A.e: The subject is "list" (singular), not "items"; the verb must agree with the singular subject, so "is" is correct.

PART_A.q: On the ACT, when a question asks for a specific numeric answer and lists possible values, the fastest strategy is often to:
o: Set up a full algebraic equation from scratch
Backsolve by plugging the answer choices into the problem
Skip the question entirely
Guess the middle value only
PART_A.e: Backsolving—testing answer choices in the original problem—is often faster than deriving equations, especially with the answers already given.

PART_A.q: For a problem with variables in the answer choices (e.g., "in terms of x"), the best strategy is to:
o: Plug in a simple number for the variable and match the numeric answer
Always choose the answer with the highest exponent
Leave the question blank
Guess based on which answer looks longest
PART_A.e: Substituting a simple number (avoiding 0 and 1) for the variable turns an abstract problem into concrete arithmetic you can check against each choice.

PART_A.q: What is the sum of the interior angles of a triangle?
o: 90 degrees
180 degrees
270 degrees
360 degrees
PART_A.e: The interior angles of any triangle always sum to 180 degrees.

PART_A.q: If f(x) = 2x + 3, what is f(5)?
"Passage mapping" on the ACT Reading section refers to:
o: Reading every word twice before answering questions
Jotting brief notes on each paragraph's main idea while reading once
Skipping the passage and only reading the questions
Memorizing the passage word-for-word
PART_A.e: Passage mapping means noting each paragraph's main idea in a few words during a single read-through, so you can quickly relocate information.

PART_A.q: A common ACT Reading strategy for passage order is to:
o: Always answer passages in the order they are printed
Tackle the passage type you find easiest first, regardless of order
Answer only the last passage
Skip whichever passage has the most questions
PART_A.e: Since all passages count equally, many test-takers do their strongest passage type first to bank points and build confidence.

PART_A.q: When a question gives a specific line number, the best approach is to:
o: Answer from memory without rereading
Read a few lines before and after the cited line for context
Only read the exact line quoted
Skip to the next question
PART_A.e: Line references are often taken out of context; reading the surrounding sentences reveals the intended meaning.

PART_A.q: A question asking "the author's tone in this passage can best be described as" is testing:
o: Detail recall
Author's purpose and tone
Vocabulary in context
Data interpretation
PART_A.e: Tone questions ask you to infer the author's attitude, which falls under author's purpose and tone strategy.

PART_A.q: The ACT Science section typically includes which three passage types?
o: Narrative, Persuasive, Expository
Data Representation, Research Summaries, Conflicting Viewpoints
Biology, Chemistry, Physics only
Multiple Choice, Free Response, Essay
PART_A.e: ACT Science passages fall into three formats: Data Representation, Research Summaries, and Conflicting Viewpoints.

PART_A.q: When reading a graph on the Science section, the most efficient first step is to:
o: Read every data point before looking at the question
Check the axis labels and units before analyzing trends
Ignore the legend
Assume the trend is always linear
PART_A.e: Identifying what each axis measures and its units first prevents misreading the graph's actual meaning.

PART_A.q: In an experimental design question, the "control group" serves to:
o: Receive the experimental treatment
Provide a baseline for comparison against the treatment group
Be excluded from data analysis
Randomize the sample size
PART_A.e: A control group is not given the experimental variable, so it provides a baseline to compare results against the treatment group.

PART_A.q: The "Conflicting Viewpoints" passage type is best approached by:
o: Reading only Scientist 1's viewpoint
Identifying where the scientists agree and disagree before answering
Averaging the two viewpoints into one answer
Skipping the passage entirely
PART_A.e: Mapping points of agreement and disagreement between viewpoints helps you quickly locate answers to comparison questions.

PART_A.q: On the optional ACT Writing test, the essay prompt presents:
o: A single fixed opinion you must agree with
An issue and three different perspectives on it
A math problem to solve in essay form
A passage to summarize only
PART_A.e: The ACT Writing prompt describes an issue and provides three distinct perspectives for the writer to evaluate.

PART_A.q: The ACT Writing essay is scored across how many domains?
o: Two
Three
Four
Five
PART_A.e: The essay is scored on four domains: Ideas and Analysis, Development and Support, Organization, and Language Use.

PART_A.q: A strong ACT essay thesis should:
o: Avoid taking any clear position
State your own perspective on the issue and preview your reasoning
Only restate the prompt word-for-word
Be placed in the final sentence of the essay
PART_A.e: An effective thesis clearly states your perspective and sets up the argument that follows, typically near the start.

PART_A.q: When analyzing multiple perspectives in the essay, you should:
o: Ignore the given perspectives and only state your own
Discuss how your view relates to at least one of the given perspectives
Rank all three perspectives without explanation
Copy each perspective verbatim
PART_A.e: High-scoring essays engage with the given perspectives, showing how the writer's own view compares or contrasts with them.

PART_A.q: Roughly how much time per question does the ACT English section allow (45 minutes, 75 questions)?
o: About 36 seconds
About 2 minutes
About 1 minute
About 5 minutes
PART_A.e: 45 minutes / 75 questions = 0.6 minutes, or 36 seconds per question.

PART_A.q: A "pacing checkpoint" strategy means:
o: Never checking the clock during the test
Periodically checking that you're on pace (e.g., halfway through time = halfway through questions)
Only checking the time at the very end
Ignoring section time limits
PART_A.e: Checking progress at set intervals (like the midpoint) helps you catch and correct pacing problems before time runs out.

PART_A.q: The "two-pass strategy" on a timed section means:
o: Answering every question twice for accuracy
Answering easier questions first, then returning to harder ones
Reading the passage twice before any questions
Taking the section twice
PART_A.e: The two-pass strategy skips time-consuming questions on the first pass and returns to them after answering the easier ones.

PART_A.q: Because the ACT does not penalize wrong answers, test-takers should:
o: Leave difficult questions blank
Always guess rather than leave any answer blank
Only guess on easy questions
Skip the last five questions of every section
PART_A.e: Since there's no penalty for incorrect answers, guessing on questions you can't finish is always better than leaving them blank.

PART_A.q: ACT English questions that ask about comma usage, verb agreement, or punctuation are classified as:
o: Rhetorical Skills questions
Grammar (Usage/Mechanics) questions
Vocabulary questions
Data interpretation questions
PART_A.e: Grammar/Usage questions test mechanics like punctuation and agreement, distinct from Rhetorical Skills questions about style and organization.

PART_A.q: A math question that says "which of the following equations could represent..." is testing:
o: Pure computation only
Your ability to translate a word problem into an equation
Geometry proofs
Data collection methods
PART_A.e: This question format requires converting a described scenario into an algebraic model, a common ACT Math trap for those who skip translation.

PART_A.q: A Reading question asking "it can reasonably be inferred that..." is a:
o: Detail question
Inference question
Vocabulary-in-context question
Big-picture/main idea question
PART_A.e: Inference questions ask you to draw a conclusion the passage implies but doesn't state directly.

PART_A.q: An effective ACT study schedule typically:
o: Crams all studying into the night before the test
Spreads practice tests and review over several weeks with regular review sessions
Only involves taking the real test
Focuses on one section only, ignoring the others
PART_A.e: Spacing practice over weeks with regular review of missed questions builds retention and steadily improves scores.

PART_A.q: When reviewing missed questions, the most effective approach is to:
o: Just note the correct answer and move on
Identify why you missed it (careless error, content gap, or timing) and address the root cause
Skip review and take another practice test immediately
Only review questions you got right
PART_A.e: Understanding the specific reason for a mistake—not just the right answer—prevents repeating the same type of error.

PART_A.q: Simulating real test conditions during practice includes:
o: Taking breaks whenever you want mid-section
Using strict section time limits and minimal interruptions
Using a calculator on every section
Skipping the essay portion during practice
PART_A.e: Timing sections strictly and minimizing interruptions builds the stamina and pacing needed for the actual test day.

PART_B1.q: Which choice correctly fixes: "Each of the students have finished their homework"?
o: have finished their homework
has finished their homework
has finished its homework
having finished their homework
PART_B1.e: "Each" is singular, so it takes the singular verb "has," not "have."

PART_B1.q: An ACT English question asking whether a proposed sentence should be added to a paragraph is primarily testing:
o: Punctuation rules
Relevance and unity within the paragraph
Verb tense consistency
Word choice precision
PART_B1.e: Add/delete sentence questions test whether the sentence supports the paragraph's main idea, not grammar mechanics.

PART_B1.q: Which sentence uses "who"/"whoever" correctly?
o: Whom is going to the store?
Give the ticket to whoever arrives first.
Give the ticket to whomever arrives first.
She is the person who I trust the most, whom is rare.
PART_B1.e: "Whoever" is the subject of "arrives," so the subjective case is correct even though the whole clause is the object of "to."

PART_B1.q: What is the slope of a line passing through the points (2, 3) and (6, 11)?
If 3x - 7 = 20, what is the value of x?
A rectangle has a length of 12 and a width of 5. What is its area?
PART_B1.e: Area = length x width = 12 x 5 = 60.

PART_B1.q: On the ACT Reading section, a "vocabulary-in-context" question asks you to:
o: Define a word using outside knowledge
Determine how a word is used specifically within the passage
Identify the most common dictionary definition
Find a synonym regardless of context
PART_B1.e: These questions require using the surrounding sentence to determine the word's meaning as used in that specific passage, which is often not the most common definition.

PART_B1.q: When a Reading question does NOT give a line reference, the best strategy is to:
o: Skip the question entirely
Guess based on general impression only
Use your passage map/notes to locate the relevant section quickly
Reread the entire passage from the beginning
PART_B1.e: Efficient passage mapping lets you locate the relevant section without rereading the whole passage, saving time.

PART_B1.q: A "main idea" question on the ACT Reading section asks about:
o: A minor supporting detail
The overall point or purpose of the passage
The author's use of a single word
A statistic mentioned in paragraph two
PART_B1.e: Main idea questions test comprehension of the passage's central point, not isolated details.

PART_B1.q: On the ACT Science section, a "Research Summaries" passage typically presents:
o: A single data table with no experiments
Descriptions of one or more experiments and their results
Two scientists arguing opposing theories
Only reading comprehension text with no data
PART_B1.e: Research Summaries passages describe experiments, including methods and results, usually with figures or tables.

PART_B1.q: If a science passage shows that as variable X increases, variable Y decreases, this represents:
o: A direct relationship
An inverse relationship
No relationship
A random relationship
PART_B1.e: When one variable increases while the other decreases, that is an inverse (negative) relationship.

PART_B1.q: In a Science section question, extrapolating beyond the given data range means:
o: Reading a value directly off the table
Predicting a trend beyond the measured data points
Ignoring the data entirely
Averaging all given values
PART_B1.e: Extrapolation means projecting a trend to estimate values outside the range that was actually measured.

PART_B1.q: On the ACT Writing test, a strong essay should address the given perspectives by:
o: Ignoring all three perspectives and inventing a new one
Analyzing the perspectives and presenting your own, with reasoning
Simply restating each perspective without analysis
Choosing a perspective at random without support
PART_B1.e: Scorers reward essays that engage with the provided perspectives, explain their strengths/weaknesses, and support the writer's own view with reasoning.

PART_B1.q: Which of the following most strengthens an ACT essay's development score?
o: Repeating the thesis in every paragraph
Providing specific, relevant examples and explaining their significance
Using long words even if imprecise
Keeping every paragraph to one sentence
PART_B1.e: Development is scored on how well ideas are explained and supported with specific reasoning and examples, not on vocabulary or repetition.

PART_B1.q: If you are running low on time near the end of the ACT Math section, the best strategy is usually to:
o: Leave remaining questions blank
Guess the same letter for all remaining questions since there is no penalty for wrong answers
Go back and redo every completed question
Stop working immediately
PART_B1.e: Since there is no guessing penalty, filling in an answer for every remaining question (a consistent letter is efficient) maximizes expected score versus leaving blanks.

PART_B1.q: A "pacing checkpoint" during a timed ACT section means:
o: Stopping the section early
Checking at set intervals (e.g., after 15 questions) whether you're on pace to finish
Skipping checkpoints entirely
Only checking the time once at the very end
PART_B1.e: Pacing checkpoints let you compare your progress to the time elapsed so you can adjust speed before it's too late.

PART_B1.q: An ACT Math question asking you to find where two lines intersect is testing:
o: Systems of equations
Probability
Data representation only
Vocabulary
PART_B1.e: Finding the intersection point of two lines is solving a system of equations, either by substitution or elimination.

PART_B1.q: An English question that asks you to choose the most concise, non-redundant phrasing is testing:
o: Subject-verb agreement
Conciseness/wordiness
Punctuation placement
Pronoun-antecedent agreement
PART_B1.e: These questions test the ACT's preference for the shortest option that preserves the sentence's meaning.

PART_B1.q: When building an ACT study schedule, it's most effective to:
o: Study only the day before the test
Focus exclusively on your strongest section
Prioritize review of your weakest question types based on practice test data
Avoid taking any full-length practice tests
PART_B1.e: Targeted review of weak areas, identified through practice test results, produces the most score improvement per hour studied.

PART_B1.q: Simulating real test conditions during a practice test includes:
o: Taking breaks whenever you want
Using a timer and taking only the official section breaks
Skipping the Science section entirely
Looking up answers as you go
PART_B1.e: Realistic practice means timing each section accurately and only taking breaks where the real test allows them, to build stamina and pacing skills.

PART_B2.q: Which sentence correctly uses an apostrophe?
o: The dog wagged it's tail.
The dogs' owner arrived late.
The dogs owner's arrived late.
Its' tail wagged happily.
PART_B2.e: "Dogs'" (plural possessive) correctly shows the owner belongs to multiple dogs; "it's" is a contraction for "it is," not a possessive.

PART_B2.q: A question asking "the passage suggests that the narrator feels ___ about the decision" is testing:
o: Literal recall of a stated fact
Inference based on textual evidence
Vocabulary definition
The author's biography
PART_B2.e: "Suggests" signals an inference question — the answer isn't stated directly but must be reasonably drawn from the text.

PART_B2.q: In the ACT Science section, a "Conflicting Viewpoints" passage is best approached by:
o: Assuming all scientists agree
Identifying where each viewpoint agrees and disagrees before answering questions
Skipping the passage since it has no data
Answering questions before reading either viewpoint
PART_B2.e: Mapping the points of agreement and disagreement between viewpoints up front makes it much faster to answer comparison questions.

PART_B2.q: On the ACT Writing test, the essay is scored on a scale of:
o: 1 to 6 per domain, averaged
2 to 12 total
1 to 36 total
1 to 4 domains only, no numeric score
PART_B2.e: Each of the four domains is scored 1-6 by two graders (2-12 combined per domain), and the domain scores are averaged for the reported essay score.

PART_B2.q: The ACT Reading section gives 35 minutes for 40 questions across four passages. About how much time should you budget per passage?
o: 4-5 minutes
8-9 minutes
15 minutes
20 minutes
PART_B2.e: 35 minutes / 4 passages is roughly 8-9 minutes per passage, including reading and answering.

PART_B2.q: A Science question asking "based on the data in Table 1, which of the following best predicts the result at 50°C" is testing:
o: Pure vocabulary recall
Interpolation/extrapolation from data trends
Random guessing strategy
Essay-writing skills
PART_B2.e: Predicting an untested value from a data trend is a classic interpolation or extrapolation question type.

PART_B2.q: After completing a full-length ACT practice test, the most valuable next step is to:
o: Immediately take another full practice test
Review every missed question to understand the specific error type
Ignore the results and move on
Only check your overall score, not individual questions
PART_B2.e: Reviewing missed questions to identify patterns (careless error vs. content gap vs. timing issue) drives targeted improvement more than repeated blind testing.

PART_B2.q: Which choice best corrects the wordy phrase: "due to the fact that it was raining"?
o: due to the fact that it was raining
because it was raining
being that it was raining
for the reason that it was raining
PART_B2.e: "Because it was raining" conveys the same meaning far more concisely; the ACT favors the shortest correct option.

PART_B2.q: A circle has a radius of 4. What is its circumference (in terms of π)?
o: 4π
8π

PART_C.q: Written response: choose TWO concepts from different units and construct an argument connecting them. Cite specific evidence from each.
o: Names both concepts precisely, gives concrete evidence for each, and explains the causal/logical bridge
Lists the two topics without connecting them
Describes only one concept in detail
Gives a personal opinion with no course evidence
PART_C.e: Strong responses anchor every claim in specific unit content.

workedExamples.title: Fixing a comma splice
workedExamples.prompt: Which revision fixes this sentence? 'The test was long, students finished early.'
steps: Spot the problem: two complete sentences are joined by only a comma, which is a comma splice.
List the fixes: add a coordinating conjunction after the comma, replace the comma with a semicolon, or split it into two sentences.
Check meaning: the second clause contrasts with the first, so 'but' is the best conjunction.
workedExamples.answer: The test was long, but students finished early. (A semicolon or a period would also be correct.)

workedExamples.title: Finding the main idea
workedExamples.prompt: How can you answer a main-idea question quickly on the ACT Reading test?
steps: Read the first and last sentences of each paragraph to see how the passage develops.
State the passage's point in one sentence of your own before looking at the choices.
Eliminate choices that are too narrow (one detail) or too broad (go beyond the passage).
workedExamples.answer: Choose the answer that matches your own summary and covers the whole passage without adding new claims.

workedExamples.title: Reading a graph
workedExamples.prompt: A graph of plant height against days of sunlight shows heights of 4, 6 and 8 cm at 2, 4 and 6 days. What trend does it show?
steps: Read the axes first: days of sunlight are on the horizontal axis and height on the vertical axis.
Compare the points: each 2 extra days of sunlight adds 2 cm of height.
Describe the relationship in words: as sunlight days increase, height increases at a steady rate.
workedExamples.answer: Height increases linearly with days of sunlight (about 1 cm per day).

workedExamples.title: Building a thesis
workedExamples.prompt: Write a thesis for the prompt: 'Should schools start later in the morning?'
steps: Take a clear side instead of describing both views.
Give two reasons you can develop in separate paragraphs.
Make sure the claim is arguable, not just a fact.
workedExamples.answer: Schools should start later because teenagers' sleep cycles shift later and well-rested students learn and behave better.

workedExamples.title: Pacing the Reading test

Plan to leave a minute at the end to bubble in any blanks.

workedExamples.title: Reviewing a practice test
workedExamples.prompt: After finishing a practice test, how should you review it to improve your score?
steps: Sort each missed question by cause: content gap, careless error or timing.
Redo the missed questions without looking at the answer key.
Make a short plan to practice the weakest category before the next test.
workedExamples.answer: Reviewing by type of error raises scores faster than simply taking more tests.

workedExamples.title: NOT and EXCEPT questions
